units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
For a piecewise linear concave function \(f(x) = \min_{i} (a_i x - b_i)\), the subdifferential at \(x^*\) is the convex hull of gradients of active pieces: \(\partial f(x^*) = \{\sum_{i \in I(x^*)} \lambda_i a_i : \lambda_i \ge 0,\; \sum \lambda_i =1\}\) where \(I(x^*)=\{i: f(x^*) = a_i x^* - b_i\}\). A point \(x^*\) maximizes \(f\) over \(\mathbb{R}^n\) iff \(0 \in \partial f(x^*)\).

Modeling transfer: Any max-min objective of this form (e.g., worst-case throughput, robust profit, or conservative capacity constraints) can be tackled by subgradient optimization. A subgradient is any \(a_i\) with \(i \in I(x^*)\). Moving along a subgradient may not locally increase \(f\) (as shown by example), but a small step in any subgradient direction reduces the Euclidean distance to some optimal solution. Thus a subgradient algorithm with appropriate step sizes converges to an optimum. This caution is important: do not reject a direction merely because the objective seems to drop at the current iterate; it can still improve proximity to optimality. The method applies directly to concave nondifferentiable functions arising in piecewise linear resource allocation, congestion control with multiple bottlenecks, or Lagrangian dual problems where the dual function is the minimum of affine pieces.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
Lagrangian relaxation is applied to integer programs with coupling constraints (e.g., demand assignment \(\sum_j y_{ij}=1\)) by dualizing them into the objective, leaving a subproblem over a simple feasible set \(Q\). The resulting dual function \(z(\lambda) = \min_{x \in Q} (c - \lambda A)x + \lambda b\) is piecewise linear concave, maximized via subgradient optimization. A subgradient at \(\lambda^0\) is \(s = b - A x^*\), where \(x^*\) solves the relaxation.

Practical step-size rules for multiplier updates \( \lambda^{t+1} = \lambda^t + \alpha_t s^t\): geometric series \(\alpha_t = \alpha_0 \rho^t\) or \(\alpha_t = (\text{target} - z(\lambda^t))\rho^t / \|s^t\|^2\) with \(0<\rho<1\); halving \(\alpha\) every fixed number of iterations often suffices. Zero subgradient rarely occurs, so branch-and-bound embedding stops after a fixed iteration limit or when the integrality gap \(z(\lambda^t) - \text{best primal} < 1\). Final multipliers are used to construct primal feasible solutions (e.g., greedy facility opening using reduced costs) and to fix variables via reduced prices.

An exact alternative is constraint generation (Kelley's cutting-plane method) that solves the Lagrangian dual by adding constraints derived from extreme points of \(Q\).

For uncapacitated facility location, relaxing demand constraints gives a closed-form subproblem: \(z(u) = \sum_j \big[ \sum_i (c_{ij} - u_i)^+ - f_j \big]^+ + \sum_i u_i\), with subgradient \(s_i = 1 - \sum_j y_{ij}^*\), where \(y_{ij}^* = 1\) if \(x_j^*=1\) and \(c_{ij}-u_i>0\), else \(0\). This decomposition pattern—dualizing linking constraints to yield independent per-facility decisions—transfers to set covering and partitioning problems with assignment structure.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
In uncapacitated facility location (UFL), binary variables \(x_j\) open facilities and \(y_{ij}\) assign clients, with profit equal to revenue minus fixed costs. The LP relaxation is tightened by adding variable upper-bound constraints \(y_{ij} \le x_j\) and lifted cover inequalities; the FCPA (Fenchel cutting-plane algorithm) generates such cuts. Reduced-price fixing eliminates variables when \(|\text{reduced cost}| \ge \text{gap}\). For set covering, a greedy heuristic selects at each step the column that minimizes cost per newly covered row.

A max-min objective \(f(x)=\min_i(a_i^T x - b_i)\) over a convex set \(C\) is handled by subgradient steps; normalizing subgradients avoids bias from coefficient magnitudes and accelerates convergence. In 0‑1 knapsack-based cuts, a cover inequality can be lifted to include extra variables (e.g., \(x_1+x_6+x_7\le 1\) lifts to \(x_1+x_6+x_7+x_9\le 1\)). Fixed-charge network flow problems can be reformulated as multicommodity arc-path models.

Implementation caution: without cutting planes, branch-and-bound on a 33-variable problem remained open after 1000 nodes; adding FCPA cuts solved it optimally in 77 nodes.

units.summary:
This memo extracts transferable modeling and algorithmic constructs.

Projection-based subgradient method for nonnegative variables: given a step direction s_t and step size θ, the update y_{t+1} = x_t + θ s_t is projected onto the feasible region C = R^n_+ via x^{j}_{t+1} = max(x^j_t + θ s^j_t, 0). This is standard for large-scale LPs derived from combinatorial problems (e.g., Held-Karp lower bounds for TSP).

Integrality conditions for set packing: the polytope {x ∈ R^n_+ : A x = 1} with 0-1 matrix A is integral if and only if A is a network matrix (see Proposition 4.1). Balanced and totally balanced matrices extend this property; strong chordal graphs supply strong elimination orderings that characterize totally balanced matrices, enabling integer solutions for covering/packing problems on such graphs.

Network matrix recognition: a maximal network submatrix can be identified via recognition algorithms; this supports decomposition and reduction of integer programs to tractable network flow subproblems.

A facility location / dominating set template: given a graph with node weights c, service demands r_j, and coverage distances d_ij (here, number of edges on the path), the minimum-weight set of service nodes that can cover every node is a weighted dominating set with demand thresholds—a reusable pattern for UAV logistics or air mobility service placement under range constraints.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
Graphs model pairwise relationships via nodes and edges; bipartite partitions (e.g., workers–jobs, customers–facilities) appear in assignment and facility location problems. Directed graphs (digraphs) capture one-way arcs. Node–edge incidence and adjacency matrices allow linear formulations of connectivity, degree, and flow constraints. Paths and cycles generate constraints: the set of nodes in a path is a walk without repetition; cycles are closed paths of length ≥3. Trees are connected acyclic graphs with m−1 edges and a unique path between any two nodes, useful for spanning-tree bounds.

Data representation restrictions: instances must be described by a list of basic elements (e.g., edge–cost pairs); an algorithm cannot assume an exponential list of all tours or subsets as input, forbidding trivial enumeration.

The group problem relaxation transforms an IP into a maximum-weight path problem over a modular digraph. Let \( a_j \) be integer coefficients, \( k \) a modulus. The relaxed problem maximizes \(\sum (c_j - u a_j)x_j + ub\) subject to \(\sum a_j x_j \equiv b \pmod{k}\), \(x_j \in \mathbb{Z}_+\), where \(u = p/k\) is a dual-feasible LP multiplier. Boundedly positive costs \(c_j - u a_j \le 0\) prevent unboundedness. This pattern links Lagrangian relaxation with dynamic programming on a state graph.

Stochastic models: random graphs with independent edges (probability \(q\)) let us analyze greedy heuristics—for facility maximization, greedily picking max-degree nodes is almost surely optimal when the number of facilities grows slowly. For p-median in the plane with uniformly random points, asymptotic optimal values can be sharply estimated, guiding heuristic evaluation.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
A modular equality constraint over nonnegative integers can be encoded as a directed graph where nodes are residue classes modulo a chosen integer k. For a constraint ∑ a_j x_j = b (mod k) with x_j ∈ Z₊, construct a digraph with nodes 0,…,k−1. For each variable j, add an arc from node d to node φ_k(d + a_j) (where φ_k is the remainder modulo k). Feasible assignments correspond to directed walks from node 0 to φ_k(b): each use of variable j traverses its corresponding arc.

This yields a modeling pattern: solving the modular relaxation reduces to finding a directed path (dipath) from 0 to the target residue; directed cycles represent homogeneous solutions (∑ a_j x_j ≡ 0 mod k) that can be added without changing the residue. The full integer equality regains exactness only if the dipath plus a nonnegative combination of cycles satisfies the original equation exactly. This decomposition (dipath + cycles) is used in Gomory’s group problem for integer programming.

The node-arc incidence matrix of the digraph (each column has one +1 and one −1) can enforce flow conservation. When arc weights are nonpositive, a maximum-weight dipath problem on this small state-space graph solves the group relaxation. A caution: a dipath solution may not directly lift to a feasible integer point for the full equation; additional cycle variables may be necessary, and the objective must account for both the dipath and cycle contributions.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
Shortest-path problems: given digraph with arc weights, find minimum-weight directed s–t path. Nonnegative weights: Dijkstra (O(|V|²)) builds a tree of minimum-weight paths from source by iteratively labeling the node with smallest tentative distance; relies on the property that subpaths of optimal paths are optimal. With negative weights but no negative cycles: Bellman–Ford (O(|V|·|A|)) iterates |V| times over all arcs; if distances still decrease at iteration |V|, a negative cycle exists. For reconstruction, maintain predecessor pointers.

Group problem: integer program min{cx : Σ a_j x_j ≡ b (mod k), x ∈ Z₋ⁿ}. Reducing with dual multiplier yields a longest-path problem on a cyclic digraph with nodes 0,…,k−1; arcs represent choosing an item and consume its residue a_j mod k with weight c_j. The optimal value function is linear in b plus a periodic correction term. This converts a modular knapsack into a dynamic-programming/shortest-path form.

Minimum-weight branching/spanning tree: select arcs to form a directed tree rooted at a specified node (branching) or an undirected spanning tree. Polynomial LP formulations exist. The node-arc incidence matrix for s–t path flows is totally unimodular; unit flow out of s, unit flow into t, conservation elsewhere, and x ≥ 0 yields integer solutions without explicit integrality constraints. This pattern extends to network design where flow conservation encodes connectivity.

units.summary: Minimum spanning tree (MST) is exactly solved by a greedy algorithm: order edges by non-decreasing weight, include each if it creates no cycle. The same algorithm applies for maximum-weight spanning tree (order decreasing) and maximum-weight acyclic subgraph (stop after the last positive-weight edge). The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) is relaxed via minimum-weight 1-tree: an MST on all nodes except node 1, plus the two cheapest edges incident to node 1. Lagrangian relaxation transforms edge costs to c_ij − λ_i − λ_j, with dual variables λ updated by subgradient: step proportional to (2 − degree of node i in the 1‑tree). This provides a lower bound for branch‑and‑bound. Branching eliminates subtours or fractional edges; violated subtour elimination constraints are separated by detecting connected components in the support graph. 2‑matching inequalities (odd‑set constraints) are separated via max‑flow algorithms, tightening the relaxation. The 1‑tree relaxation plus subgradient optimization and dynamic constraint generation is a reusable pattern for routing problems with degree constraints (exactly two edges per node) and connectivity requirements. When building trees on sparse graphs, efficiency is gained by considering only edges incident to nodes not yet included.

units.summary:
A digraph of nodes and directed arcs models flow: each node i has supply b_i (b_i<0 is demand), with total supply zero. Each arc (i,j) has capacity d_ij and unit cost w_ij. Flow variables x_ij must satisfy node conservation (outflow minus inflow equals b_i) and 0 ≤ x_ij ≤ d_ij.

Minimum-cost flow: minimize sum w_ij x_ij. The transportation special case uses a bipartite graph; supply nodes have b_i>0, demand nodes b_j<0. The maximum-flow problem introduces source s, sink t, sets b_i=0, w_ts = -1, d_ts = ∞, and maximizes x_ts.

A primal-dual algorithm for transportation shifts costs via duals u_i, v_j to obtain nonnegative reduced costs w_ij – u_i – v_j, then uses a maximum-flow subproblem to push flow along zero-reduced-cost arcs until supply is met. The equivalent minimum-cost-path augmentation constructs a network with source arcs to supply nodes (capacity = supply, cost 0), demand arcs to sink (capacity = demand, cost 0), and infinite-capacity arcs (i,j) cost w_ij. Augment along a shortest s–t path. When flow x_ij > 0, add reverse arc (j,i) with cost –w_ij and capacity ∞. Flow augmentation terminates with optimal solution when all supplies are satisfied.

For general network flow, the node-arc incidence matrix of a connected digraph with m nodes has rank m–1. The simplex method exploits spanning-tree bases: the basic arcs form a spanning tree, and pivots use tree operations. This structure enables efficient network simplex implementations.

These directly support spatio-temporal network models for UAV logistics and air mobility.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
Maximum flow problem: given a directed graph with arc capacities \(d_{ij}\), source \(s\), sink \(t\). Decision variables: arc flows \(x_{ij}\). Constraints: \(0 \le x_{ij} \le d_{ij}\), flow conservation at all nodes except \(s,t\), and total flow out of \(s\) equals flow into \(t\) (the flow value \(F\)). Objective: maximize \(F\). Minimum cut: partition \((U, V\setminus U)\) with \(s\in U, t\notin U\); cut capacity is sum of \(d_{ij}\) for arcs from \(U\) to \(V\setminus U\). Duality: \(\max F = \min\) cut capacity. Integrality: if all capacities are integer, an integer maximum flow exists.

Solution via augmenting-path algorithm: construct residual digraph with forward arcs where \(x_{ij}<d_{ij}\) and reverse arcs where \(x_{ij}>0\). Label nodes (predecessor, allowed increment) and scan; if sink is labeled, augment flow along the path. When no unscanned labeled node remains, the current flow is maximum and the set of scanned nodes \(U\) defines a minimum cut. Implementation caution: without care, the number of augmentations can equal the flow value \(F\). Using breadth-first search to always select a shortest augmenting path bounds the total augmentations by \(m \cdot n\) (arcs × nodes), ensuring polynomial runtime. This duality and augmentation pattern can directly model bottleneck capacities in air corridors or UAV delivery networks and check throughput feasibility.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
Transportation problem: bipartite digraph with sources (supply ai) and sinks (demand bj), arc from every source to every sink; missing arcs assigned large cost. Total supply must equal total demand for feasibility, else add dummy sink with zero cost and demand equal to surplus. Decision variables xij ≥ 0, flow from source i to sink j. LP: min sum cij xij s.t. row sums = ai, column sums = bj. Dual variables ui (source) and vj (sink), dual feasible if cij - ui - vj ≥ 0. Complementary slackness: xij > 0 implies cij - ui - vj = 0.

Primal-dual algorithm alternates between max-flow and dual update. Given dual feasible (u,v), define admissible arcs where reduced cost = 0. Solve max-flow from super-source to super-sink with arc capacities equal to ai on source side, bj on sink side, infinite on admissible arcs. If flow equals total supply, optimal. Else, from final labels in max-flow (reachable set from source), compute δ = min reduced cost for arcs from labeled source nodes to unlabeled sink nodes. Update dual variables: for labeled source nodes decrease ui by δ, for labeled sink nodes increase vj by δ; reduced costs update accordingly. At least one new admissible arc appears, flow can increase. Method guarantees integral optimal solution since all capacities are integral and max-flow yields integral flows. Whole process terminates after at most total supply iterations, with one max-flow solve per dual update. Applicable as a decomposition for min-cost flow problems with bipartite structure, useful in logistics and assignment planning.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
The transportation problem and its variants offer reusable modeling patterns for UAV logistics where supplies (e.g., package inventory at depots) and demands (delivery points) are large integers. A binary scaling technique decomposes the problem into \(k = \lceil \log_2(\max(a_i,b_j))\rceil\) stages. At each stage \(p\), supplies and demands are truncated to \(\lfloor a_i/2^{k-p}\rfloor\), so unsatisfied amounts are at most the number of nodes \(m\). The previous stage’s flow is doubled, and a dummy sink (or source) balances the network. Each stage uses \(O(m)\) augmentations, and dual variables carry over to warm-start the next stage. Total augmentation count is \(O(m \log U)\) instead of \(O(U)\) where \(U\) is the total supply. This directly applies when drone package volumes are large; complexity then depends on network size, not total packages.

Integral polyhedra give a condition for LP relaxations to yield integer solutions. For a matrix \(A\), the system \(\{y \ge 0: yA \le w\}\) has the integer rounding property if the polyhedron \(Q\) is integrally decomposable. Many network flow matrices satisfy this, meaning assignment or path-based UAV routing formulations can be solved as continuous LPs without branch-and-bound, as long as right-hand sides \(w\) are integer. The primal-dual algorithm maintains reduced costs and augments along shortest paths; it guarantees finite convergence and can be paired with scaling. When modeling airspace capacity constraints or vertiport slot assignments, check whether the constraint matrix inherits integral decomposability from an underlying network structure to avoid integer variables.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary: A minimum-cost network flow model has nodes with supply/demand \(b_i\) (sum zero) and directed arcs \((i,j)\) with cost \(c_{ij}\) and optional capacity \(u_{ij}\). Flow variables \(x_{ij}\) satisfy flow conservation \(\sum_j x_{ij} - \sum_j x_{ji} = b_i\), \(0 \le x_{ij} \le u_{ij}\). The node-arc incidence matrix is totally unimodular, so a basis corresponds to a spanning tree of \(m-1\) arcs among \(m\) nodes; after a leaf-root permutation the basis submatrix becomes lower triangular with \(\pm1\) diagonals, guaranteeing integral flows when supplies are integral. The primal simplex algorithm works directly with tree structures: dual potentials \(y_i\) are defined by \(y_i - y_j = c_{ij}\) on tree arcs with \(y_{\text{root}}=0\); a non-tree arc enters if its reduced cost \(\hat{c}_{ij}=c_{ij}-(y_i-y_j)<0\). Adding the arc creates a unique cycle; flow is increased by \(\theta\) on forward arcs and decreased by \(\theta\) on reverse arcs, where \(\theta = \min\{x_{ij}\}\) on opposite-orientation arcs. The limiting arc leaves the basis; \(\theta=0\) gives degeneracy. Upper bounds are handled implicitly by excluding at-bound arcs from the tree. Dual updates are local, recalculated only in the subtree cut by the leaving arc. Efficient tree representations are essential for performance. This pattern transfers to UAV logistics and urban air mobility: network subproblems with flow conservation, integrality via unimodularity, and spanning-tree bases can be embedded in decomposition frameworks for rapid localized optimization.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
For integer programming sets S (binary vectors, tours, packings), the convex hull conv(S) is a polyhedron; maximizing a linear objective over S is equivalent to solving a linear program over conv(S). Producing a linear inequality description of conv(S) is the central modeling task.

A polyhedron P = {x : Ax ≤ b} has dimension k if there exist k+1 affinely independent points in P. The equality set M= consists of constraints satisfied at equality by all x in P; these equalities determine the affine hull. A facet-defining valid inequality is one that is tight for exactly dim(P) affinely independent points of P.

For the node packing (stable set) problem on a graph G = (V,E), node choices are binary variables x_j. The edge constraints x_i + x_j ≤ 1 and nonnegativity define a basic polyhedron. If H ⊆ V induces an odd hole (chordless cycle of odd length ≥5), the inequality sum_{j∈H} x_j ≤ floor(|H|/2) = (|H|-1)/2 is valid and gives a facet of the node-packing polytope for that subgraph. This inequality cannot be implied by edge constraints, and it can cut off fractional extreme points from the edge-only relaxation. To lift such a valid inequality to a facet of the full conv(S), one must often search for further points that satisfy it at equality; otherwise it defines a lower-dimensional face that can be “tilted” to a stronger facet. This pattern—starting with a valid inequality tight for a structured subset, then extending to a full facet—transfers to many polyhedral combinatorics contexts.

units.summary: A polyhedron \(P = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : A x \le b,\; A^= x = b^=\}\) has dimension \(\dim(P) = n - \operatorname{rank}(A^=, b^=)\). A valid inequality \(\pi x \le \pi_0\) defines a face; it is a facet exactly when the face dimension equals \(\dim(P)-1\). The facets give a minimal description: every inequality representing a face of dimension \(< \dim(P)-1\) is redundant and can be discarded. Two inequalities are equivalent descriptions of the same facet if one is a positive scalar multiple of the other plus a linear combination of the equality rows \((A^=, b^=)\). This equivalence is key when adding cutting planes: a candidate cut is useless if it lies in the conic hull of existing constraints modulo the equalities. For a polyhedron contained in \(\mathbb{R}^n_+\) the constraint matrix typically has full column rank, so zero-dimensional faces (extreme points) exist, and the set equals the convex hull of its extreme points plus the conic hull of its extreme rays. To reduce a formulation, retain one representative from each facet equivalence class and drop any inequality that does not support a facet. An inequality that is not tight at an inner point of a lower-dimensional face is redundant. These rules help build compact linear and integer programming models and verify that newly generated valid inequalities are not already implied.

Optimization and separation are polynomially equivalent for many families of polyhedra: an efficient separation subroutine implies polynomial solvability of linear optimization over the polyhedron. This equivalence underpins delayed constraint generation as a complete algorithm, not just a heuristic.

Consequently, if an integer programming problem is NP-hard, the underlying polyhedral family cannot have bounded rank. This structural property guides complexity analysis and may inform the design of finite cutting-plane methods.

Once an EPT representation is obtained, sign orientations are verified on submatrices with at most two nonzeros per column. If a matrix passes these checks, it is a network matrix and the corresponding tree/digraph pair can be constructed explicitly.

units.summary:
Lifting enables construction of a valid inequality for a binary set S by extending a known valid inequality for a restriction where one variable is fixed to 0 (or 1). If ∑_{j=2}^n π_j x_j ≤ π_0 is valid for S ∩ {x_1 = 0}, then α_1 x_1 + ∑_{j=2}^n π_j x_j ≤ π_0 is valid for S when α_1 ≤ π_0 − ζ, with ζ = max{∑_{j=2}^n π_j x_j : x ∈ S ∩ {x_1 = 1}}. The maximum lift, α_1 = π_0 − ζ, preserves full strength: if the original inequality defines a facet of the restricted convex hull, the lifted inequality defines a facet of conv(S). An analogous rule lifts from the x_1 = 1 restriction.

Sequential lifting extends this to multiple variables. Order matters: the coefficient obtained for a variable is smallest when it is lifted last and largest when lifted first. Different orders produce different facet-defining inequalities; some facets cannot be generated by any sequential order but require simultaneous lifting of several coefficients—equivalent to finding an extreme point of a higher-dimensional polar polytope.

In practice, exact ζ is often hard to compute, so upper bounds on it are used to obtain valid (but possibly weaker) coefficients. This approach provides a direct method to prove a given inequality is facet-defining by showing it matches a maximally lifted lower-dimensional facet or by solving a linear system over affinely independent points.

units.summary:
For the symmetric traveling salesman polytope on m nodes (n = m(m-1)/2 edge variables), incidence vectors of tours define the feasible set. The natural IP formulation uses binary variables per edge, degree constraints (exactly two incident edges per node), and an exponential family of subtour elimination constraints (SECs): sum_{e in E(W)} x_e ≤ |W|−1 for all nonempty proper subsets W.

Modeling insight: SECs are facet-defining for the TSP polytope when |W| ≤ floor(m/2). Beyond that size, the constraint for W is equivalent to that for V\W, so only subsets up to half the nodes need be considered. This cuts the number of non-redundant SECs in exact separation schemes. The polytope dimension is n−m, meaning the degree equalities already reduce the affine hull.

Transferable pattern: In any routing or coverage problem requiring a single cycle covering all nodes, the SEC family provides a strong linear description. Branch-and-cut implementations should separate SECs efficiently via maximum-flow or Gomory-Hu tree procedures, prioritizing subsets with |W| ≤ m/2. For structured integer programs, a facet proof often proceeds by showing that any hyperplane containing a set of tours satisfying the inequality at equality must be a linear combination of degree constraints plus the target inequality, a technique reusable for deriving other valid inequalities in combinatorial optimization.

This is a shortest-path problem on a digraph whose nodes are integer vectors modulo Δ (|det Δ| nodes) and arcs correspond to nonbasic columns; it is a knapsack with modular arithmetic when only one diagonal entry of Δ is nontrivial.

Any feasible IP solution corresponds to a path from node 0 to node R b (mod Δ). When p > 0, the optimal IP solution corresponds to a k-th best path. A dual descent algorithm starts with \(u_i=\max_j c_{ij}\) and cyclically reduces each \(u_i\) to the next smaller \(c_{ij}\) while maintaining the feasibility constraints, then applies an interchange (increase a \(u_i\) with multiple tight facilities, restart descent) to escape local minima. For knapsack‑type subproblems where items are ordered by descending profit‑to‑weight ratio, adopt depth‑first branching with fixed variable sequence: first set x_k = 1, then x_k = 0. If a node is pruned by bound or an optimal solution is found when x_k = 1, do not branch on x_k = 0; the bound ordering guarantees no improvement. Backtrack by flipping the most recent variable set to 1 to the 0 branch, skipping redundant searches.

Generalized upper‑bound (GUB) constraints ∑_{j∈Q_i} x_j = 1 with disjoint Q_i call for balanced branching. Instead of singling one fractional variable, split Q_i into two subsets Q_i^1 and Q_i^2 of nearly equal cardinality, and branch on ∑_{j∈Q_i^1} x_j = 0 versus ∑_{j∈Q_i^2} x_j = 0. This yields a more balanced tree than conventional variable branching.

Piecewise linear functions f(y) represented by convex combinations of breakpoints can be enforced without binary variables inside branch‑and‑bound. Maintain the SOS2 condition by branching on the sum of λ variables to left or right of a breakpoint: if λ_k > 0, branch on ∑_{j=0}^{k-1} λ_j = 0 or ∑_{j=k+1}^{t} λ_j = 0.

Node selection: before a feasible solution exists, maximize the estimated optimal value (best estimate). Once a solution is known, use quick improvement: choose the node maximizing (Z_est − Z_LP)/(Z_est − Z_best) to find better solutions rapidly. For branching variable selection, user‑defined priorities reflecting decision hierarchy (e.g., strategic commitments before operational details) are robust; otherwise, compute degradation penalties using reduced‑cost estimates of the LP decrease if the variable is forced integral, then branch on the fractional variable with largest estimated cost in the direction (up/down) of smaller penalty.

units.summary:
The excerpts present a finite variant of the Gomory fractional cutting-plane algorithm for integer programming, using lexicographic ordering to guarantee convergence. The core reusable modeling knowledge lies in the solution method and its safeguards, not in domain entities.

**Optimization Problem:** Integer linear program (IP) with bounded feasible set, solved by iteratively tightening its LP relaxation (RP_t) with Gomory cuts.

**Key Method: Lexicographic Dual Simplex for Cutting Planes**
- Maintain the LP in the form: max x_0, subject to x_i + sum_{j in H} a_i^j x_j = a_i^0 (i=0,...,n), with x_i ≥ 0, and trivial identity rows x_j – x_j = 0 for nonbasic j in H.
- A basic solution is lexicographically largest feasible if all nonbasic columns satisfy a^j ≥ 0 (componentwise) and a_i^0 ≥ 0 for i=1,...,n. If initially a^j has zero first component and nonnegative later components, a redundant constraint y + sum_{j in H} x_j = d (d large) is appended to make all a^j lexicographically positive.
- Dual simplex pivot: when a row p has a_p^0 < 0, choose leaving variable x_p. Let H_p^- = {j : a_p^j < 0}. If empty, no feasible solution. Otherwise, select entering variable x_k by a lexicographic ratio test: a_k / (–a_p^k) >_L a_j / (–a_p^j) for all j ≠ k in H_p^-, where >_L denotes lexicographically larger. This rule preserves a^j ≥ 0 in the next basis and strictly reduces the lexicographic value of the right-hand side vector (a^0) at each pivot, preventing cycling.

**Integration with Cuts**
- Solve RP_t to obtain its lexicographically largest solution (x_0^*, x^*). If fractional, locate the first component x_s ∉ Z. Let a_t = (x_0^*, …, x_{s-1}^*, ⌊x_s^*⌋, d, …, d). The cut a_0 – Σ a_j x_j ≤ 0 (derived from the fractional row) is added, ensuring that any integer feasible solution is lexicographically ≤ a_t, and the new lexicographically largest LP solution strictly decreases. This yields a finite sequence of cuts.

**Implementation Cautions**
- Initial basis must be dual feasible with a^j ≥ 0; the redundant constraint trick guarantees this.
- The lexicographic ratio test (3.4) must be implemented carefully because columns can contain identity vectors; ties are impossible by construction.
- The method assumes boundedness; otherwise the dual feasible basis may not exist.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
For integer programs with many strong valid inequalities, use a fractional cutting-plane algorithm (FCPA) on the LP relaxation. Start with core constraints Ax≤b. Each iteration: solve the current LP, then run separation over inequality class ℘. If a violated inequality is found, add it; repeat until no violation. In uncapacitated facility location (UFL), the essential strong inequalities are Y_ij ≤ X_j (variable upper bounds). Separation: for each j, if max_i Y_ij > x_j, add the cut(s). Typically only a small subset is needed (9 of 30 in the UFL example).

If the final LP solution is fractional, embed into branch-and-bound (Phase 2) using the generated cuts as a reformulation. Before branching, fix variables via reduced costs: given an incumbent integer objective z̄, for a nonbasic variable at lower bound with reduced cost c_j ≤ 0, if z_LP + c_j ≤ z̄, fix it to the lower bound; at upper bound with c_j ≥ 0, if z_LP – c_j ≤ z̄, fix to the upper bound. This eliminates variables.

Pattern: Weak assignment-type formulations benefit from the strong inequality Y_ij ≤ X_j, generated dynamically. FCPA plus branch-and-bound yields a strong cutting-plane algorithm. A mixed-integer program with a single integer variable creates a branch-and-bound tree with at most three nodes. For pure integer feasibility, an alternative cutting-plane strategy maintains integrality and dual feasibility, then adds Gomory cuts to achieve primal feasibility, yielding a finitely convergent algorithm.

Weak formulation aggregates Y_ij without per-facility upper bound, allowing X_j = (1/m)∑_i Y_ij* and ignoring fixed costs—closed-form LP optimum uses only best net-revenue facility per client. units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
In many facility location, sensor coverage, and resource allocation problems, the objective is a monotone submodular set function v(Q) under a cardinality bound |Q| ≤ p. Submodularity means marginal gains decrease as the set grows: for S ⊂ T, v(S∪{k})−v(S) ≥ v(T∪{k})−v(T). A classic example is v(Q)=∑_i max_{j∈Q} c_ij where each client i gains the best profit among selected facilities.

A greedy heuristic that iteratively adds the element giving the largest immediate increase achieves a performance guarantee Z_G / Z ≥ 1 − ((p−1)/p)^p ≥ 1 − 1/e ≈ 0.63, where Z is the optimal value. This bound is tight. The greedy solution can be improved by an interchange (local search) heuristic that swaps one open facility with one closed facility as long as the objective improves; its worst-case ratio is p/(2p−1). For submodular covering problems, a dual-ascent greedy heuristic yields an H(d)-approximation, where d is the maximum element-level increment.

Primal-dual heuristic pairs use complementary slackness: for a 0‑1 packing problem max{cx : Ax ≤ 1, x∈{0,1}^n} and its linear relaxation dual, a primal heuristic can be guided by dual variables to generate feasible solutions. The interchange heuristic may get stuck at local optima; simulated annealing escapes by occasionally accepting worsening moves.

These patterns transfer directly to UAV placement for maximum coverage, charging station deployment, and hub location where the objective is submodular.

units.summary:
Submodular set functions satisfy the diminishing-returns inequality \(v(S\cup\{k\})-v(S) \ge v(T\cup\{k\})-v(T)\) for \(S\subseteq T\). When maximizing a nondecreasing submodular function subject to a cardinality constraint \(|Q|\le p\), the greedy algorithm (iteratively adding the element with largest marginal gain) achieves an approximation guarantee of \(1-((p-1)/p)^p\), which tends to \(1-1/e\). This guarantee can be proved via a dual linear program. The pattern directly transfers to any location, sensor-placement, or influence-maximization problem with a budget of \(p\) facilities and spatial diminishing returns.

For general combinatorial maximization \(\max_{Q\subseteq M} c(Q)\) where local search stalls, simulated annealing provides an escape mechanism. From current solution \(Q^i\), a neighbor \(Q'\in N(Q^i)\) is drawn. If \(c(Q')\le c(Q^i)\), the move is accepted with probability \(\exp((c(Q')-c(Q^i))/a_i)\). The temperature is decayed multiplicatively: \(a_{i+1}=a_i(1-\rho)\) with \(0<\rho<1\). Convergence requires symmetric, reachable neighborhoods with equal selection probability, but empirical performance depends critically on the neighborhood structure and cooling schedule; exponential worst-case convergence cautions against trusting asymptotic guarantees without experimentation.

units.summary: Dynamic programming (DP) models for knapsack and lot-sizing transfer directly to UAV resource allocation. In 0‑1 knapsack, the value function \(z_k(d)\) for first \(k\) items and remaining capacity \(d\) follows \(z_k(d)=\max\{z_{k-1}(d),\; c_k+z_{k-1}(d-a_k)\}\), yielding an \(O(nb)\) pseudo‑polynomial algorithm; the same recursion can be viewed as a longest‑path problem on a graph with nodes \((k,d)\), each arc encoding a binary inclusion/exclusion decision. For unbounded integer knapsack the recursion simplifies to \(z(d)=\max_j\{c_j+z(d-a_j)\}\), also \(O(nb)\), modeling repeated use of a resource‑consuming activity (e.g., multiple identical drone trips). The uncapacitated lot‑size problem (ULS) obeys a strong structural property: an optimal solution satisfies \(S_{t-1}Y_t=0\) and when production occurs, \(Y_t\) equals the sum of demands for an integer number of consecutive periods. This eliminates continuous state tracking and reduces complexity to \(O(T^2)\). For UAV battery charging or energy storage, the same zero‑inventory property cuts the state space: never simultaneously store and replenish, and each charge event covers a block of future energy demands. The traveling salesman DP defines state \((S,j)\) (visited set, current node) with recursion \(f(S,j) = \min_{k\in S\setminus\{j\}}\{f(S\setminus\{j\},k)+c_{kj}\}\), a template for sequencing drone delivery stops. Caution: these DP algorithms are pseudo‑polynomial; running times depend on the magnitude of capacity or demand parameters, so scaling the discretization is critical for practical use.

The uncapacitated lot-sizing (ULS) problem minimizes production, setup, and holding costs over time with deterministic demand. State variable is entering inventory S_{t-1}; decision Y_t is production quantity with associated binary setup. The symmetric traveling salesman problem (TSP) is modeled with degree-2 constraints, upper-bound constraints, and subtour elimination inequalities. Stronger cuts such as 2-matching and comb inequalities tighten the LP relaxation. A fractional cutting-plane algorithm (FCPA) iterates: solve LP, separate violated subtour, 2-matching, and comb inequalities, add them, and resolve. Branch-and-bound then uses the final LP bound and a heuristic cutoff (e.g., nearest-neighbor or greedy with 2-interchange) to find the optimal tour. In a 67-city instance, 19 initial subtour elimination constraints were added at the root, but branch-and-bound later required additional cuts to eliminate 2-matching solutions that undercut the tour value, demonstrating that root-only cutting planes may be insufficient for large instances.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary: Knapsack problems model resource allocation with items having weight \(a_j\) and profit \(c_j\) under capacity \(b\); variables are nonnegative integers or binary. The LP relaxation for 0‑1 knapsack is solved by ordering items by decreasing \(c_j/a_j\) until capacity is exhausted, yielding a fractional critical item with ratio \(\lambda^*\); knowledge of \(\lambda^*\) reduces the LP to a linear pass. Dynamic programming by profit yields minimum weight needed to achieve profit \(t\): \(w(t)=\min_j\{a_j+w(t-c_j)\}\) for \(t>0\). When profit coefficients are large, scaling replaces \(c_j\) by \(\lfloor c_j/K\rfloor\); the scaled problem solves in \(O(n Z_{\text{LP}}/K)\) and guarantees relative error \(\le 1-K/\min c_j\). This is efficient only when \(K\) is large, i.e. profits are big, opposite to the greedy heuristic that performs best with small profits. The scaling/rounding (SR) heuristic partitions items by a profit threshold \(\theta=(\epsilon/4)Z_{\text{LP}}\), applies scaled DP to high‑profit items and greedy rounding to the rest, combining via filling residual capacity with the best‑ratio low‑profit item. It achieves \((1-\epsilon)\) optimality in \(O(n\epsilon^{-2})\) time. The group problem relaxes an integer program \(Ax=b\) via a dual vector \(u\) with nonnegative reduced costs, a unimodular matrix \(R\), and a diagonal modulus \(\Delta\); the resulting minimum‑weight path on a congruence digraph of size \(|\det \Delta|\) gives a relaxation. Cautions: scaling requires \(K\le \epsilon\min c_j\); dynamic programming profit range must be bounded; SR partitioning threshold depends on the LP optimum. These patterns transfer to any resource‑capacity allocation with integer decisions and separable linear objectives/constraints.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
The 0-1 knapsack problem (maximize sum of selected item values subject to a single linear capacity constraint) models many resource-allocation tasks in UAV logistics: choosing delivery tasks under battery budget, packing payload items, or selecting mission waypoints within time limits. Its LP relaxation is solved in linear time by identifying the critical ratio λ* = c_j / a_j that evenly divides items into forced 1 and forced 0 sets, with at most one fractional item. This yields integrality patterns: when the LP solution is unique, all items with c_j/a_j > λ* are fixed at 1, those below at 0; the break item takes a fractional value to exhaust the resource.

After solving the LP relaxation, two reduced-cost elimination tests can fix integer variables before branching. Test 1 (weaker): if the LP objective minus |reduced cost| does not exceed a known lower bound, fix the variable to its LP bound. Test 2 (stronger): recompute an upper bound assuming the variable is forced to the opposite bound, using a linear knapsack LP with adjusted capacity; if that bound is no better than the incumbent, fix permanently. These tests use the same ratio ordering and run fast. For subproblem optimization within branch-and-bound for larger assignment, routing, or scheduling models (e.g., UAV fleet tasking with capacity constraints), embedding this O(n) LP solver and elimination rules accelerates node processing.

The primal heuristic after LP also applies: fix LP-1 variables, then greedily insert remaining items ordered by nonincreasing c_j/a_j until capacity is exhausted. This gives a feasible solution quickly. When using knapsack components in broader models, storing items sorted by efficiency and maintaining the break-point index allows incremental updates as bounds change, a useful pattern for column generation or dynamic programming subproblem solvers.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary: Binary integer programs with decision variables \(x_j\in\{0,1\}\) and constraints \(\sum a_j x_j \le b\) (converted to equalities via slacks) can be attacked by a primal heuristic that pivots from the LP relaxation basis. The integer infeasibility of basic regular variables is measured as \(q = \sum_{i\in N'} \min(x_i,\,1-x_i)\) and primal infeasibility as \(h = \sum_{i\in N'} \max(0,\,-x_i,\,x_i-1)\). A feasibility search (Phase I) applies pivots that preserve primal feasibility while reducing the number of basic regular variables or decreasing \(q\); if no such pivot exists, it rounds to the nearest integer, forces all fractional variables to zero, and then complements (flips) nonbasic regular variables individually or in pairs to reduce \(h\). A local improvement phase (Phase II) fixes variables using a reduced-profit criterion (based on LP reduced costs) and then complements up to three nonbasic regular variables to improve the objective. This structure embeds naturally into fractional cutting-plane and branch‑and‑bound algorithms: cover inequalities \(\sum_{j\in C} x_j \le |C|-1\) for any cover \(C\) with \(\sum_{j\in C} a_j > b\) serve as strong valid inequalities. A caution: on structured problems such as pure 0‑1 knapsack, the heuristic collapses to greedy (first fractional variable swapped with the slack, halted when an item does not fit), offering no advantage over simpler methods; it is best kept for large, complex instances where other approaches struggle.

units.title: Integer and Combinatorial Optimization
units.summary:
**Modeling memo (TSP relaxations, heuristics, and bounds)**

**Core problem:** Symmetric traveling salesman problem (TSP) on complete graph \(G=(V,E)\) with edge weights \(c_e \ge 0\). Find minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle (tour).

**Key relaxations (lower bounds):**
- **2-matching:** degree-2 at every node; allows subtours. Characteristic vector \(x \in \{0,1\}^{|E|}\) with \(\sum_{e\in\delta(v)} x_e =2\) for all \(v\). Solvable as assignment problem.
- **1-tree:** spanning tree on \(V\setminus\{1\}\) plus two edges incident to node 1. A tour is simultaneously a 2-matching and a 1-tree.
- **Subtour elimination constraints** cut off disconnected solutions; can be added dynamically (cutting plane/separation).

**Decision variables:** \(x_e \in \{0,1\}\) indicating edge inclusion. Objective: \(\min \sum c_e x_e\).

**Heuristics with performance guarantees (require triangle inequality):**
- **Double spanning-tree:** duplicate MST edges, find Eulerian cycle, shortcut to tour. Weight \(\le 2\times\text{OPT}\).
- **Spanning-tree/perfect-matching:** MST + min-weight perfect matching on odd-degree nodes, then Eulerian shortcut. Weight \(\le \frac{3}{2}\times\text{OPT}\).

**Key property:** Under triangle inequality, shortcutting a walk never increases total weight, giving performance bounds.

**Exact algorithm pattern:** Branch-and-bound using assignment problem (2-matching) relaxation; branching on edge exclusion/inclusion by deleting corresponding edges/nodes in the bipartite representation.

**Caution:** Without triangle inequality, no polynomial-time heuristic can guarantee any constant approximation ratio unless P=NP.

units.summary:
A constraint matrix that is totally unimodular (TU) guarantees that the polyhedron {x | Ax ≤ b, x ≥ 0} is integral for all integral right-hand sides b. Memo: Submodularity-Based Capacity Modeling and Optimization for UAV Logistics

A nondecreasing submodular set function f(S) on N (e.g., fleet units, airspace zones) models diminishing returns and joint capacity limits. The polymatroid P(f) = {x ∈ R₊ᴺ : ∑_{j∈S} x_j ≤ f(S) ∀S⊆N} captures load limits where total activity over any subset cannot exceed f(S). When f is integer-valued, P(f) is integral, yielding integer optimal solutions for linear objectives. The separation problem (checking x* ∈ P(f) or finding a most violated inequality) reduces to submodular function minimization: min_S (f(S) – ∑_{j∈S} x_j*). This enables cutting-plane methods for optimization over such capacity systems. The rank function r(a) = max{∑ x_j : x∈P(f), x≤a} equals min_T (f(T) + ∑_{j∉T} a_j), useful for throughput maximization under per-element caps.

This admits a cutting-plane (Benders-like) solution.

Caution: Submodular maximization is hard; verify structure before assuming efficiency. Use the polynomial submodular minimization oracle for polymatroid separation.

Network matrices—arc-dipath incidence matrices of directed trees—are TU and can be solved directly by network simplex without node-arc reformulation. Recognition: recursively decompose the row intersection graph, build an edge-path tree, and check sign orientations. A (0,±1) matrix with at most two nonzeros per column is TU precisely when its rows can be bipartitioned according to sign patterns.

Interval matrices (columns with consecutive ones) are TU; a covering problem min{cx : Ax ≥ b, x ∈ Z₊ⁿ} with such a matrix becomes a min-cost flow. Reduced costs p_j = u A_j – c_j (u = c_B A_B⁻¹) are non‑positive. The resulting problem min ∑ p_j y_j subject to the modular constraint is a longest‑path problem on a digraph with ∏ δ_i nodes (residue vectors modulo Δ). An arc for each nonbasic column j goes from node d to φ_Δ(d + R a_j) with weight p_j.

Such a walk decomposes into a dipath achieving the target residue plus nonnegative cycles (homogeneous solutions). The dipath alone may not lift to a feasible basic solution; cycle variables must be added to satisfy exact equality x_B = A_B⁻¹(b – A_N y) ≥ 0. units.summary:
Flow-based models for UAV logistics use a digraph: supply nodes are vertiports/depots with positive inventory (b_i>0), demand nodes are delivery points (b_j<0), and arcs represent spatio-temporal flight segments with capacity d_ij (airspace throughput, vertiport slot limits) and cost w_ij (energy, time). Variables x_ij are drone flow counts, subject to flow conservation (outflow minus inflow equals supply) and bounds 0 ≤ x_ij ≤ d_ij. Total supply must equal total demand; add a dummy sink with zero cost if needed.

The primal-dual transportation algorithm solves the min-cost flow: maintain duals u_i (source) and v_j (sink) such that reduced costs c_ij – u_i – v_j ≥ 0. Admissible arcs have zero reduced cost. Build an auxiliary max-flow network with a super-source connected to supply nodes (capacity = supply), super-sink from demand nodes (capacity = demand), and infinite capacity on admissible arcs. If max-flow equals total supply, optimal; otherwise, from labeled nodes compute δ = min reduced cost from labeled sources to unlabeled sinks. Update duals (decrease u_i for labeled sources by δ, increase v_j for labeled sinks by δ), making at least one new arc admissible, and repeat. Integer supplies and capacities guarantee integer flows.

For large package volumes (U total packages), binary scaling reduces augmentations to O(m log U): truncate supplies/demands in stages, double previous flow, warm-start duals. Reverse arcs with cost –w_ij are added dynamically to allow rerouting.

When adding airspace or vertiport capacity constraints, check whether the constraint matrix is totally unimodular (TU)—often true for network flow matrices—so LP relaxation yields integer solutions without branching. A reusable capacity-planning template is the cut condition: an integral flow ≤ capacity d exists iff for every node subset U, total supply in U ≤ capacity of arcs leaving U. This certifies feasibility before optimization and guides capacity expansion decisions.

Two inequalities define the same facet if one is a positive scalar multiple of the other plus a linear combination of the equality rows; this equivalence identifies redundant cuts and prevents generating cuts already in the conic hull of existing constraints. The polar of a full‑dimensional polytope translates extreme points directly into facet inequalities: if the polytope contains the origin in its interior, its normalized polar has constraints given by the primal extreme points, and vice versa. In UAV logistics, vertiports are binary open variables \(X_j\); fixed-charge arcs carry continuous flows \(y_{ij}\le u_{ij}X_j\), tightened by per-destination disaggregation \(z_{ijk}\le|b_k|X_{ij}\). Conflict avoidance is modeled with node packing \(x_i+x_j\le 1\), odd-cycle, and clique constraints. Routing uses binary edge variables with degree and cutset subtour elimination (avoid weak MTZ).

Totally balanced covering matrices allow greedy algorithms; polymatroid constraints via submodular minimization handle joint fleet/airspace capacities. units.title: Introduction to Linear Optimization
units.summary: The source codifies linear optimization in a way directly useful for modeling complex operational systems. It details how to transform non‑linear but convex piecewise-linear objectives (e.g., absolute deviation penalties, time‑varying delivery costs) into linear programs via epigraph reformulation with auxiliary variables. The geometry of polyhedra links extreme points to basic feasible solutions, a property that justifies vertex‑search methods and column‑generation schemes for large‑scale routing or airspace assignment. Degeneracy is a practical hazard: Bland’s rule and lexicographic pivoting provide anticycling safeguards when constraints introduce redundant faces. The two‑phase method supplies a general way to find an initial feasible solution when artificial infrastructure (drones, vertiports) must be activated, crucial for models with tight time‑window and battery state‑of‑charge balances. Concrete templates—diet blending, multi‑period production planning, cyclic nurse scheduling, pattern classification via separating hyperplanes—generalize to resource mix, fleet deployment, crew pairing, and safety region filtering. Column‑geometry Simplex insights advise keeping column generation in mind for pricing flight segments. Finally, Fourier‑Motzkin elimination projects out variables, helpful for pre‑computing conflict‑free airspace corridor envelopes. Implementation caution: naive inclusion of all pairwise separation constraints explodes matrix size; explicit projection or cutting‑plane methods should be considered.

units.title: Introduction to Linear Optimization
units.summary:
Linear programming minimizes a linear cost c'x subject to linear constraints, all of which can be reduced to the form Ax ≥ b. Maximizing c'x is equivalent to minimizing –c'x; equality constraints become two inequalities; unrestricted variables are expressed as the difference of two nonnegative variables. The standard form min c'x s.t. Ax = b, x ≥ 0 is used for simplex and interior-point algorithms.

Three transferable modeling templates:
1. Resource allocation: maximize Σ c_j x_j s.t. Σ_j a_{ij} x_j ≤ b_i, x_j ≥ 0, where b_i is the limit on resource i and a_{ij} is the amount needed per unit of good j. Directly models production, bandwidth sharing, or airspace capacity allocation.
2. Minimum cost network flow: nodes have external supply/demand b_i; flow on arcs incurs unit costs, with conservation constraint net outflow = b_i. Special cases include shortest path, maximum flow, and assignment, capturing UAV routing and commodity movement through hub networks.
3. Linear classifier: find vector x and threshold x_{n+1} such that a_i' x ≥ x_{n+1} for class‑1 examples and a_i' x ≤ x_{n+1} – ε for class‑2 examples (a small margin ε replaces strict inequality). This pattern enforces separation constraints useful in trajectory deconfliction or anomaly detection.

When implementing, always convert to standard form to leverage efficient solvers. Sign restrictions like X_j ≥ 0 are special cases where a is a unit vector and b = 0.

units.title: Introduction to Linear Optimization
units.summary:
Standard form linear programs minimize \(c'x\) subject to \(Ax = b\), \(x \ge 0\). Each column \(A_j\) of \(A\) is a resource vector; the decision variables \(x_j\) are nonnegative amounts of those resources combined to synthesize the target vector \(b\) at minimum cost \(c_j\) per unit. Any general linear program can be reduced to this form by two transformations: replace a free variable \(x_j\) with \(x_j^+ - x_j^-\), where both new variables are nonnegative; and convert an inequality \(\sum a_{ij}x_j \le b_i\) into an equality by adding a nonnegative slack variable \(s_i\) (subtract a surplus variable for \(\ge\) constraints). These steps preserve feasibility and optimal cost.

The dual variables \(p_i\) obtained from an optimal basis \(B\) as \(p' = c_B'B^{-1}\) are shadow prices: the marginal cost of increasing the \(i\)-th requirement \(b_i\). Complementary slackness imposes that any resource \(j\) used at a positive level (\(x_j^* > 0\)) must satisfy \(c_j = p'A_j\). In a diet-model interpretation, this means a food used to synthesize an ideal nutritional target is priced consistently in the direct food market (cost \(c_j\)) and the imputed nutrient market (value \(p'A_j\)). This pattern generalizes to resource-allocation problems with exact demand satisfaction and cost minimization.

The dual simplex method exploits that the primal optimality condition \(p'A \le c'\) is equivalent to dual feasibility. When a dual feasible basic solution is available, the method works by maintaining dual feasibility while driving toward primal feasibility, offering an alternative to the primal simplex algorithm.

Each variant is solved with pessimistic supply values, then dual variables yield shadow prices and allowable right-hand-side ranges to identify revenue bottlenecks. Unconstrained mode: memory dual = 0, disk drives dual = 23.52—prioritize disk drives. The approach shows product-mix optimization with alternative bills-of-materials, sensitivity-driven bottleneck resource focus, and handling supply uncertainty via worst-case scenario re-optimization plus parametric range analysis. Continuous decision variables are used because demands are in thousands, making integrality negligible.

units.title: Introduction to Linear Optimization
units.summary:
A linear programming problem minimizes a linear cost function cᵀx over a polyhedron defined by linear equalities and inequalities. The feasible set is the intersection of halfspaces. Optimal solutions, when they exist and the feasible set has at least one corner, occur at extreme points (corners); multiple optimal solutions may exist, forming a bounded or unbounded face. The optimal cost may be unbounded below (–∞) or the feasible set empty.

Standard form problems (min cᵀx subject to Ax = b, x ≥ 0) can be visualized by reducing to the (n–m)-dimensional affine subspace where equality constraints hold, leaving only nonnegativity constraints to shape the feasible region.

Fourier-Motzkin elimination projects a polyhedron onto a lower-dimensional subspace by eliminating a variable. Rewrite all inequalities to isolate the variable, yielding upper bounds, lower bounds, and inequalities not involving it. Pair each lower bound with each upper bound to generate new constraints independent of the eliminated variable. This yields the exact projection but can cause an exponential increase in the number of constraints, making it impractical for large instances aside from small or specially structured problems.

These core patterns—corner optimality, projection-based dimension reduction, and the combinatorial cost of variable elimination—transfer directly to modeling tasks where polyhedral feasible sets arise.

units.title: Introduction to Linear Optimization
units.summary:
A linear system \(Ax = b\) has a unique solution iff \(A\) is square and invertible, which is equivalent to nonzero determinant, linearly independent rows/columns, and existence of the inverse \(A^{-1}\). The solution is given componentwise by Cramer’s rule: \(x_j = \det(A_j)/\det(A)\) where \(A_j\) replaces column \(j\) with \(b\).

Basis matrix updates in the simplex method are performed via elementary row operations, which correspond to left‑multiplication by an invertible matrix \(Q = I + D_{ij}\) where \(D_{ij}\) contains a single off‑diagonal entry \(\beta\). A sequence of such operations is equivalent to left‑multiplying by an invertible matrix, enabling efficient recomputation of \(B^{-1}\) when one column of the basis changes.

A square Leontief matrix (each column has at most one positive entry) is productive if some \(x \ge 0\) gives \(Ax > 0\). Productive Leontief matrices are invertible with nonnegative inverse, a structural property transferable to input‑output production models.

A finite family of polyhedra in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) has a common point if and only if every \(n+1\) of them have a common point (Helly’s theorem). For a stochastic matrix \(P\) (nonnegative, row sums equal 1), duality guarantees a nonzero nonnegative solution to \(p'P = p'\), i.e., an invariant distribution, which can model steady‑state probabilities in Markov chain constraints.

units.title: Introduction to Linear Optimization
units.summary: The complexity of operations underpinning optimization algorithms must be assessed via worst-case arithmetic operation counts. Big-O notation (and its counterparts Ω, Θ) provides a rigorous way to classify growth: solving n linear equations or inverting an n×n matrix via Gaussian elimination requires O(n³) operations. This cubic growth means doubling problem size increases work roughly eightfold. Algorithms that terminate in polynomial time (O(n^k) for fixed k) scale tractably with hardware advances; those requiring exponential time (O(2^cn)) become intractable even for modest n. These facts drive modeling decisions: avoid formulations that demand repeated dense matrix inversions for large n, exploit sparsity or decomposable structure to reduce effective dimension, and when comparing solution methods, rely on worst-case operation bounds rather than elusive average-case estimates. In practical OR modeling, a linear programming solver’s per-iteration cost is governed by such linear algebra kernels, so recognizing O(n³) bottlenecks prompts decomposition (e.g., Benders, Dantzig-Wolfe) or approximation to maintain computational viability.

units.summary:
In linear optimization models with uncertain or changing data, sensitivity analysis provides a systematic method to update solutions without full re-optimization. When a current basis is optimal, a small change in any single entry of the cost vector c, right-hand side b, or constraint matrix A preserves optimality if the feasibility condition (\(B^{-1}b \ge 0\)) and the optimality condition (reduced costs \(\bar{c}' = c' - c_B' B^{-1} A \ge 0'\)) remain satisfied. This yields intervals of allowable change where the same basis stays optimal.

Adding a new variable: compute its reduced cost from the current dual solution; if negative, append the column and continue the primal simplex. Adding a new constraint: test feasibility; if violated, introduce an artificial variable with a large penalty \(M\) and form an auxiliary tableau to restore feasibility via the dual simplex method.

When changes are large enough to violate basis conditions, the underlying basis changes. The optimal cost as a function of b is piecewise linear convex on the set where the primal is feasible, and any optimal dual solution is a subgradient. The optimal cost as a function of c is piecewise linear concave. Changes to a basic column of A lead to a perturbed basis matrix \(B + \delta E\); its inverse can be approximated as \(I - \delta B^{-1}E\) for small \(\delta\), and primal/dual variables update accordingly.

When b(θ) causes a basic variable to become zero, apply the dual simplex method to regain feasibility; an anticycling rule is needed to avoid cycling when primal degeneracy exists. These techniques reduce computation in dynamic re-planning settings like drone routing under demand or weather shifts.

units.summary:
Memo: Product-Mix LP with Multi-Level Assembly

A paper company manufactures pads of paper, 5‑packs (5 pads + small notebook), and 20‑packs (20 pads + large notebook). Each pad and notebook requires known times on a paper machine and supervisory time, and incurs a direct material cost. Packaging each bundle consumes packager time and supervisory time. Available amounts of paper‑machine time, supervisory time, and packager’s time are constants b1, b2, b3.

Decision variables: quantities of pads, 5‑packs, and 20‑packs (continuous).  
Objective: maximize total profit = Σ (selling price – total direct cost) × quantity.  
Total direct cost = sum of pad and notebook material costs (packaging adds no material cost).  
Constraints: for each resource, Σ (per‑unit consumption) × quantity ≤ available amount. Per‑unit consumption for a bundle is computed from its constituents (e.g., a 5‑pack uses 5·1 + 2 paper‑machine minutes, 5·1 + 0.75 + 1 supervisory minutes, etc.).

Transferable modeling patterns:
- The dual variable of a resource constraint yields its marginal value (e.g., an extra supervisory minute).  
- The reduced cost of a product not in the optimal mix shows the minimum price increase required for it to become profitable—directly answering “lowest viable selling price” without re‑optimizing.  
- A hiring decision (e.g., part‑time supervisors at $8/hour) is evaluated by comparing the wage rate with the marginal value per hour (dual value × 60). If dual value exceeds wage, hiring is worthwhile.  
- The formulation pre‑computes resource coefficients for final products, avoiding explicit intermediate variables for components while remaining valid for multi‑level assembly problems; it extends naturally to cases with shared intermediate parts.

This pattern applies whenever resource-constrained production includes assembled goods, enabling rapid economic sensitivity analysis via dual variables and reduced costs.

units.summary: Linear optimization offers directly transferable modeling patterns for UAV logistics and urban air mobility. Network flow constructs (capacitated arcs, flow conservation, node capacities, circulation) capture vehicle routing with side constraints. Assignment and bipartite matching allocate vehicles to tasks; stable matching handles preference-based pairing. Fleet assignment and column generation select vehicle types and schedules. Set covering, packing, and partitioning model task coverage, resource scheduling, and conflict avoidance. Integer programming (branch-and-cut, branch-and-price) enforces routing side constraints, sequencing with setup times, and vehicle selection. Lagrangean relaxation and decomposition (Benders, Dantzig-Wolfe) separate routing from assignment by relaxing linking constraints, enabling large-scale optimization. Duality and sensitivity analysis yield marginal costs and robustness to demand shifts. For implementation, sparse revised simplex or interior-point methods handle large networks; anticycling rules (smallest subscript) and degeneracy management are critical. Preprocessing, candidate list pivoting, and reinversion improve performance. Stochastic programming and robust counterparts address demand and wind uncertainty, while dynamic programming solves sequential scheduling under precedence constraints.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary: In cutting stock and bin packing problems, a naive integer programming formulation that assigns items to indistinguishable stock units (e.g., standard pipes) creates massive symmetrical solutions and is computationally intractable. A compact column-generation formulation replaces assignment variables with pattern variables γⱼ, each representing how many times a particular cutting pattern is used. Constraints then require that the sum over patterns of the number of times each ordered length appears in a pattern meets demand. The objective minimizes the total number of patterns (or stock units). The master LP is solved with an initial small set of patterns. New patterns are generated by solving a knapsack subproblem: maximize the reduced cost (e.g., sum of dual prices of demand constraints times item counts in the pattern) subject to fitting within the stock length. The knapsack solution yields a column appended to the master. This pattern-generation approach generalizes: in aircrew scheduling, patterns are rosters (paths in a space-time network); in vehicle routing, patterns are feasible routes. Subproblems become shortest-path or resource-constrained shortest-path problems. The same structure applies when the master is a set covering/set partitioning problem. Implementation caution: the initial master must be small, and column generation must eventually branch to integer solutions (branch-and-price). Symmetry in original assignment models is avoided by aggregating indistinguishable resources into pattern counts.

units.summary:
Domain entities: products, machines (grinders, drills, borers, etc.), raw oils (vegetable/non-vegetable), storage, time periods, maintenance events. Operational actors: production planners, blending managers.

Problem types: multi-period linear/integer programming for production planning, blending, and maintenance scheduling. Decision variables: production, sales, inventory, purchase, and usage quantities; binary variables for ingredient usage or machine downtime. Objectives: maximize profit (revenue minus raw material and storage costs) or minimize redundancy. Constraints: capacity limits (machine hours, refining volumes); inventory balance linking periods; blending specifications (linear hardness within bounds); if an ingredient is used then at least a minimum amount (binary \(d_i\) with \(u_i \ge 20 d_i\) and \(u_i \le UB d_i\)); at most three oils per month (\(\sum d_i \le 3\)); conditional usage (if VEG1 or VEG2 used then OIL3 must be used, enforced by \(d_1 \le d_5\) and \(d_2 \le d_5\)). Maintenance scheduling makes machine available hours variable per period, with constraints ensuring each machine is serviced.

Solution methods: branch-and-bound; using a known feasible integer solution as a cut-off to prune nodes. Matrix generators reduce errors and simplify validation; report writers extract dual values. Dual information: shadow prices give marginal value of extra capacity; reduced costs show the price reduction needed for a non-basic raw material to enter the basis, guiding procurement decisions. Cautions: impose large finite upper bounds on variables to avoid unboundedness and help debugging; experiment with solver options for difficult models.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary: A linear programming model for product mix maximizes profit contribution subject to capacity constraints (grinding, drilling, manpower). Decision variables are production quantities; constraints are linear inequalities on resource usage. The optimal solution typically has at most m non-zero variables (m = number of constraints). Shadow prices on constraints give the marginal value of a small capacity increase, valid only when changing one right-hand side at a time and within a bounded range. Reduced costs on variables indicate the minimum profit increase needed to make an unprofitable product worth producing. Right-hand side ranges define how far a single capacity can change before the shadow price interpretation breaks; beyond these limits or for simultaneous changes, parametric programming is required. Parametric programming introduces a parameter θ that scales a change column added to the right-hand side, enabling efficient analysis of coordinated capacity expansions (e.g., adding one grinding machine and one worker together). For UAV logistics and urban air mobility, these patterns transfer directly: decision variables can represent flight frequencies or cargo volumes; constraints model airspace sector capacities, vertiport slots, battery recharge availability; shadow prices estimate the value of an extra landing slot or battery swap station; right-hand side ranges prevent overextrapolation of marginal values when scaling infrastructure; parametric programming assesses fleet and facility co-expansion scenarios. Always verify that changes respect single-parameter range limits unless parametric methods are used.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
This memo distills modeling patterns from a LP blending example (food manufacture) and its multi‑period extension.

**Domain entities:** raw oils of two categories (vegetable VEG1, VEG2; non‑vegetable OIL1, OIL2, OIL3), final blended product PROD. Periods (months) with purchase, usage, and storage decisions.

**Decision variables:** tons of each oil bought, used, and stored per month; tons of final product produced per month.

**Objective:** maximize net profit = sales revenue (150 £/ton product) minus raw‑oil purchase costs minus storage cost (5 £/ton·month).

**Constraints (single‑period):**
- Refining capacities: vegetable total ≤ 200 tons, non‑vegetable total ≤ 250 tons (separate production lines).
- Hardness limits (3–6) via linear blending: weighted hardness of inputs must lie between lower and upper bounds multiplied by product quantity. Correct linear form: Σ a_i·x_i − U·y ≤ 0, Σ a_i·x_i − L·y ≥ 0, where a_i are hardness values, not simple absolute‑quantity constraints (avoids dimensional error).
- Continuity (mass balance): total raw oils used = product produced.

**Multi‑period extension:**
- Linking constraints for each oil each month: storage from previous period + purchases = usage + storage this period. Initial and final storage fixed (e.g., 500 tons). Storage variables appear with cost in objective.
- Separate purchase, usage, storage variables for each month, creating a 60‑constraint, 91‑variable LP (6 months, 5 oils).

**Solution methods:** LP solvable with standard simplex. GUB (generalized upper bound) extension can treat capacity rows efficiently when variable sets are exclusive. Sensitivity analysis (ranging) on cost/RHS coefficients is standard.

**Transferable pattern:** Any blending problem with quality constraints requiring linearization of proportions (Σ a_i·x_i / y) must be written as Σ a_i·x_i − bound·y ≤ 0. Multi‑period purchasing+storage becomes an inventory‑balance model with fixed initial/final stocks and per‑period linking equations.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
Memo: Reusable modeling techniques from "Model Building in Mathematical Programming."  
When a variable has a marketing limit or minimum demand, treat it as a simple bound (x ≤ U or x ≥ L) rather than a constraint row; solvers handle bounded variables more efficiently in the simplex algorithm. For double-sided limits L ≤ aᵀx ≤ U, specify a single ranged constraint: aᵀx ≤ U with range U−L, which bounds the slack variable and implicitly enforces the lower bound. Generalized upper bound (GUB) constraints of the form ∑_{j∈S} x_j ≤ M commonly appear; if many such constraints exist, exploiting GUB structure reduces solution time. Material balance constraints enforce conservation: sum of inputs minus sum of outputs = 0, possibly with loss/gain coefficients. Quality stipulations in blending problems require weighted averages of ingredient qualities to fall within limits. Modal formulation: when a small set of variables appears in several constraints, replace them by a convex combination of extreme points, using a single convexity constraint ∑ λ_i = 1 and λ_i ≥ 0, which can drastically cut model size. Caution: an unbounded objective signals a modeling error. Provide a starting solution if it is near-optimal to accelerate solve. Presolve procedures automatically reduce models, but identifying and exploiting GUB structures manually can yield additional computing savings; dual reduction may even solve a problem entirely.

Transferable modeling patterns include global constraints from constraint programming (CP) that can be adapted to integer programming (IP). The `all_different` predicate enforces distinct values; in IP this can be linearized with auxiliary binaries but is more cumbersome. `card_m(x_i | v)` requires exactly m variables to take value v. `cumulative((t_i),(D_i),(C_i),C)` models resource-constrained scheduling: jobs with start times t_i, durations D_i, and resource demands C_i cannot exceed total capacity C at any time—directly applicable to battery or airspace capacity limits in UAV routing. `circuit(x_i)` constrains a permutation to form a single complete tour, essential for vehicle routing (traveling salesman). `element(j, list, z)` returns the j-th element of a variable list, enabling inverse lookups. `lex_greater` imposes lexicographic ordering to break symmetry among identical entities, e.g., identical drones or delivery zones.

Logical conditions among 0-1 variables can be systematically linearized via Boolean algebra and big-M constraints, avoiding ad-hoc errors. Special ordered sets of type 1 (SOS1) model multiple-choice selections, and type 2 (SOS2) model piecewise linear functions. CP uses domain reduction via constraint propagation, akin to bound reduction in IP presolve, but allows domain holes. CP excels at finding feasible solutions in highly constrained combinatorial spaces; IP with LP relaxations is stronger for optimization and optimality proofs. When modeling, treat assignment as a function f(i)=j rather than binary x_ij for more compact CP formulations, then use element predicates for inversion.

Linear programs are tractable because optima occur at vertices of the feasible polytope, a property exploited by the simplex method. units.summary: In linear programming (LP), a constraint is binding if its removal changes the optimal solution; slack alone does not guarantee non-binding — a zero shadow price is the indicator. Complementary slackness holds: if a dual “cost” constraint is strict (imputed resource cost > profit contribution), the corresponding primal variable is zero (don’t produce); if a primal constraint has slack, its dual variable is zero (free good). However, a zero dual variable may also arise under alternative optima even when the constraint is binding, so do not automatically treat it as non-binding. Simple upper bounds on variables should be implemented as variable bounds, not as explicit constraint rows. Then the bound’s shadow price appears as the variable’s reduced cost, interpreted as the objective change from forcing the variable below its bound or increasing the bound. Redundant constraints may be kept for future data changes and ranging information, but quick redundancy checks are possible. Do not build the dual manually; solver output supplies shadow prices. Use these as internal accounting valuations to detect unprofitable activities in product-mix models.

This memo preserves modeling-relevant patterns from network flow structures and reformulations.

Generalized upper bound (GUB) constraints take the form sum of variables in an exclusive set equals b; any ≤ constraint with non‑negative coefficients can be scaled to this form. Recognizing many GUB sets dramatically speeds large LP solutions, especially within network components. Network models (transportation, minimum cost flow, shortest path) can be solved as LPs: the transportation table compacts sources, sinks, and unit costs; production‑inventory problems become transportation models with infinite costs for impossible time periods.

A shortest path is a minimum cost flow with one unit of supply at the start node and one unit of demand at the destination. For all single‑commodity network flow LPs (transportation, transshipment, assignment, min cost flow), integral right‑hand sides guarantee integral optimal flows without integer programming. This property breaks for multi‑commodity flows (fractional solutions possible) and for generalized networks with arc multipliers (gains/losses); the latter can represent any 0‑1 integer program. Multi‑commodity flow yields block‑angular structure treatable by Dantzig‑Wolfe decomposition.

Lower bounds on arc flow can be enforced by adding an extra node with forced external flow; upper bounds similarly with an outflow node. Reformulating a problem into a pure or near‑network form lets the GUB facility or specialized algorithms avoid expensive integer programming. Even when only a large network component exists, most variables remain integer in the LP optimum, drastically reducing IP difficulty. Models that are duals of network flow problems also inherit integral optimal solutions when the original’s objective coefficients are integer.

Cautions: dense input‑output models are untypical and can cause numerical trouble; standard simplex may need adaptation. Always check for negative cost cycles when allowing negative arc costs to prevent unboundedness.
