When constructing a mathematical programming model, prefer explicit variables over implicit substitutions unless a report writer handles interpretation, because compactness hinders error detection and solution understanding. Use mnemonic names for all variables and constraints to ease debugging.

To detect infeasibility, substitute a known feasible operating point (e.g., a past week’s plan) into the current constraints. Any violated constraint indicates an over-restrictive formulation that needs correction. Infeasibility may arise from mutually incompatible constraints rather than a single erroneous inequality.

For unbounded models, check for missing material-balance or capacity constraints; the intermediate solution printed before termination often reveals physically impossible activities such as production without raw materials. An unbounded primal implies an infeasible dual, but an infeasible primal may yield an infeasible or unbounded dual.

Build error detection into the model by converting hard constraints into soft ones: replace a constraint ∑ aⱼxⱼ ≤ b with ∑ aⱼxⱼ – u ≤ b and penalize u in the objective (negative cost for maximization, positive for minimization). This prevents artificial infeasibility while flagging violation magnitude. Validate a solvable model by optimizing multiple contrived objectives to stress-test different subsets of constraints; the resulting violations expose missing or mis-specified restrictions. Model validation should proceed iteratively, converging toward an accurate representation.

The substitution technique for process modes uses convex-combination variables λ_i to represent the output of an activity as a weighted average of extreme operating points (modes). This eliminates explicit constraints linking inputs and outputs when those relationships are fixed proportions per mode, replacing them with definitions like x_A = Σ λ_i * (coordinate of mode i). The method can substantially reduce constraint counts.

For input-output systems, balance equations enforce total output = external demand + intermediate consumption by all industries. With alternative production technologies, an LP can select the best input mix. If only one primary resource (labour) is limiting, the Samuelson substitution theorem guarantees that each industry will use exactly one technology, and that choice is invariant with respect to the bill of goods. Mixing of multiple technologies per industry becomes necessary only when there are two or more primary resources. This simplifies models: once the best technology is identified, only that column per industry need be retained for any demand scenario. Conversely, in multi-resource settings (e.g., energy and airspace capacity in UAM), technology mixing may be optimal, and process-selection variables must be retained.

units.summary:
Memo: Multiplant LP structures and decomposition patterns

Domain entities: Factories (A, B) with plant-specific processes (grinding, polishing capacities in hours/week). Products (standard, deluxe) each consume processing time and a shared raw material (kg/unit, total weekly supply 120 kg). Profit contributions by product.

Model structure: Company-wide LP maximizes total profit from production quantities x1..x4. Common row captures raw material limit summed across all plants. Diagonal blocks contain plant-specific capacity constraints. This yields a block angular structure: common rows (shared resources) + submodels (plant constraints). Without common rows, plants decouple; with them, coupling forces coordinated allocation.

Decision variables: production amounts per product per plant. Objective: sum of product contribution margins. Constraints: shared resource availability (common row), local capacity limits per plant (submodel rows).

Decomposition methods: (1) Allocation-based (Rosen): find optimal split of RHS of common rows among submodels. (2) Price-based (Dantzig-Wolfe): assign internal prices to shared resources, subtract resource usage from subproblem objectives, iterate until supply balances. This mirrors decentralized planning: head office sets internal prices; plants optimize locally; prices adjust based on total resource usage.

Additional structures: Staircase structures arise in multi-period models (converting to block angular possible). Common-column structures (dual to block angular) connect subproblems via shared variables; Benders decomposition applies. In multi-period planning, avoid artificial end-of-horizon effects by either extending the horizon or assigning terminal values to stocks.

Stochastic programs extend block angular structures to scenario trees, leading to very large models with many scenarios sharing first-stage variables.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
In two-stage stochastic programming with recourse, first-stage decisions (e.g., production quantities \(x_j\)) are made before uncertain demand is known. Demand is discretized into \(m\) scenarios \(d_j^{(r)}\) with known probabilities \(p_r\). For each scenario, second-stage recourse variables \(y_j^{(r)}\) (excess) and \(z_j^{(r)}\) (shortfall) are introduced to correct imbalances: \(x_j - y_j^{(r)} + z_j^{(r)} = d_j^{(r)}\). The objective minimizes total expected cost: \(\sum_j c_j x_j + \sum_r p_r (\sum_j e_j y_j^{(r)} + f_j z_j^{(r)})\), where \(c_j\), \(e_j\), \(f_j\) are production, excess, and shortfall costs. First-stage capacity constraints \(\sum_j a_{ij} x_j \le b_i\) couple only the \(x_j\) variables.

The LP matrix has common columns for \(x_j\) and block-angular blocks of \(y_j^{(r)}, z_j^{(r)}\) for each scenario—enabling decomposition methods. This pattern hedges against uncertainty by keeping options open, avoiding a single point forecast. Scenario trees explode when multiple stages multiply; use scenario reduction or Benders decomposition. Alternatives like maximin (conservative) or chance constraints address different risk attitudes, but the recourse model captures expected-cost minimization under quantifiable, discrete uncertainty.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
A multi-plant production problem with a common scarce resource (raw material) can be decomposed via Dantzig-Wolfe. Each factory forms a subproblem with its own local capacity constraints and product variables. The master problem aggregates proposals—columns representing extreme-point production plans from each subproblem—using convex-combination weights λ_ij that satisfy a convexity constraint (sum λ_ij = 1) per subproblem. The master retains only common constraints (raw material) and the profit contributions of each proposal.

Solution alternates between solving a restricted master (initially with a few proposals) and solving subproblems. The master’s shadow price on the common resource becomes an internal transfer price charged to subproblems. Subproblems re-optimize their local objective penalized by that price, generating new proposals (vertices). A proposal is added to the master only if its reduced cost is favorable. The process stops when no subproblem offers a new proposal; the master then yields the optimal mix of subproblem extreme points, reconstructing the optimal solution to the full model.

This pattern applies whenever a block-angular structure links independent operating units through shared resources. Caution: unbounded feasible regions require handling of extreme rays (not just vertices) to ensure correct pricing. The method avoids building a monolithic model where the number of extreme points can be astronomical.

units.summary:
LP models frequently appear as blending, resource allocation, network flow, and multi-period planning. Blending problems (petroleum, chemicals, food, mining) impose linear quality constraints on mixtures of inputs to meet specifications. Transportation and transshipment models are network LPs with flow conservation, supply, and demand constraints; they extend to distribution with depot location via integer programming. Financial portfolio selection is typically quadratic (minimize variance of return subject to expected return). Health resource allocation models suffer from uncertain input data but still inform policy. Energy scheduling (generator dispatch, hydropower) can use stochastic dynamic programming.

LP naturally extends with integer or nonlinear terms for fixed charges, economies of scale, or risk.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) provides a fundamental routing template transferable to UAV logistics and urban air mobility. The conventional integer programming formulation uses binary variables δ_ij=1 if leg i→j is traversed, minimizes total cost, and imposes assignment constraints: each node exactly one entry and one exit. These constraints alone permit subtours. Complete a priori subtour elimination is exponential, but the practical approach adds constraints lazily as subtours arise in relaxed solutions, typically requiring very few before optimality. This lazy constraint strategy is a key implementation caution.

Compact alternative formulations exist: sequential (Miller–Tucker–Zemlin) with position variables; flow-based (Gavish–Graves) using material balance; multi-commodity flow (Wong, Claus) which remarkably matches the conventional formulation’s LP relaxation strength yet has O(n³) size; time-staged models (Vajda, Fox) with stage-indexed variables. Orman and Williams (2006) rank LP relaxation strengths of eight formulations independent of instance—a crucial insight for formulation selection. The multi-commodity flow version can naturally embed additional resources like battery state-of-charge in drone routing. The supply chain integration pattern—linking sub-models’ outputs as inputs to a global profit-maximizing LP—also transfers to multimodal UAM operations. Seriation and DNA sequencing are further TSP variants.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
Domain entities: industries (sectors) producing a single homogeneous output using inputs from other industries and primary resources (labour, processing capacity); final demand (bill of goods).  
Model type: static Leontief input–output as LP. Core constraints: material balance per industry — total output \(x_i\) = intermediate demand \(\sum_j a_{ij}x_j\) + final demand \(y_i\), so \((I-A)x = y\). Primary resource limits: e.g., labour \(\sum_i l_i x_i \le L\).  
Decision variables: outputs \(x_i\) or final demands \(y_i\). Objective: maximise total output \(\sum x_i\), weighted output, or a single sector’s output. Shadow prices on primary-resource constraints yield valuations of those resources.  
Key modeling nuance: with a single technology per sector and exactly binding resource constraints the system may have a unique feasible solution — the objective then exerts no influence. Introducing alternative production processes for the same output (multiple columns per sector) permits input substitution and gives a genuine LP optimum; process mixing becomes worthwhile when multiple primary goods exist.  
Dynamic extension: time-phased version where outputs produced in one period become inputs in later periods, and investment increases future capacity, creating trade-offs between current consumption and growth. Formulation as multi-period LP.  
Aggregation caveat: combine industries only if they have similar production processes, are substitutable, or complementary; poor aggregation distorts input coefficients.  
Integer programming caution: when output variables represent indivisible goods (airplanes) and optimal values are small integers, rounding the continuous LP solution may be infeasible. Treat as IP only if variable magnitudes are small; large discrete quantities (e.g., national livestock) may safely be relaxed to continuous.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
Transportation and network flow models use nodes (sources/sinks) and arcs with unit costs. Decision variables \(x_{ij}\) represent flow from node \(i\) to \(j\). Constraints are either availability (sum out ≤ supply) and requirement (sum in ≥ demand) or node material balance: total inflow minus total outflow equals net supply (negative for sources). If total supply exceeds demand, add a dummy sink with zero cost to convert inequalities to equalities. Forbidden arcs are omitted or penalized with a large M. Capacitated problems impose bounds \(l_{ij} \leq x_{ij} \leq u_{ij}\).

The assignment problem, with unit supplies and demands, yields integer (0-1) solutions from the LP relaxation due to total unimodularity—no explicit binary constraints needed. Transshipment extends transportation by allowing flow among sources or among sinks; it reduces to a transportation problem by treating every node as both source and sink with zero availability/requirement as appropriate.

Shortest path is modeled by sending exactly one unit from origin to destination, with arc costs equal to lengths; the optimal flow path traces the shortest route. Maximum flow adds variables for external flow into sources and out of sinks, maximizing total throughput subject to upper arc capacities, again preserving integrality.

Specialized algorithms (Hungarian for assignment, Dijkstra for shortest path, Ford–Fulkerson for max/min-cost flow) exploit the network incidence matrix structure, avoiding expensive integer programming. These patterns directly transfer to UAV logistics by treating vertiports/depots as nodes, flight corridors as arcs, costs as energy or time, and capacities as airspace or landing‑slot limits.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
Project scheduling can be modeled as a directed acyclic network where arcs are activities with fixed durations and nodes mark activity start/end events. Dummy arcs (zero duration) enforce precedence without consuming time. The critical path problem seeks the minimum project completion time.

Decision variables: start time \(t_i\) for each event (node), and a project finish variable \(z\). Objective: minimize \(z\). Constraints: for each activity \(i \to j\) with duration \(d\), impose \(t_j - t_i \geq d\); a final constraint links the last event to \(z\) (e.g., \(-t_{\text{last}} + z \geq d_{\text{last}}\)). This linear programming formulation yields the longest-path solution, identifying the critical path that cannot be delayed without extending the project. Though LP-solvable, specialized algorithms (CPM, Ford-Fulkerson longest-path) are far more efficient than building and solving the LP directly.

A resource-constrained extension assigns limited resources (e.g., crews) to activities. If total resource demand exceeds capacity, activities must be delayed or stretched. This becomes an integer programming problem where binary or integer variables schedule start times or allocate resources. However, general-purpose integer programming is computationally prohibitive for realistic instances; heuristic or tailored scheduling methods are preferred. Objectives can shift to minimizing project delay under resource limits or smoothing resource usage over time. This yields a reusable template: a precedence network LP with resource capacity constraints that, when converted to integer scheduling, demands caution due to combinatorial explosion.

A linear program can be recast as a minimum-cost network flow model when all constraint coefficients can be scaled to 0 or ±1. This transformation eliminates the need for integer programming because network flow problems yield integer optimal solutions given integer external flows.

Original variables become non-tree arcs, each forming a unique polygon with tree arcs according to its non-zero rows. Feasibility hinges on the existence of such a tree where every original variable's non-zero rows correspond to a polygon in the tree—if impossible, the network reduction fails.

Arc orientation follows the sign pattern: traversing a polygon, tree arcs are directed opposite to the non-tree arc for +1 coefficients, and in the same direction for −1 coefficients. If no compatible orientation exists, a directed network cannot be built. Non-tree arcs receive unit costs equal to the scaled objective coefficients; tree arcs carry zero cost. Each node’s external flow is the sum of scaled right-hand sides of rows whose tree arcs leave the node minus those whose tree arcs enter.

After solving the network flow model, variable values may need rescaling. This pattern is applicable to any linear program with the required zero/±1 coefficient structure, often found in logistics, assignment, and distribution problems originally containing only upper-bound constraints. The procedure provides a computational shortcut by avoiding general simplex or integer algorithms.

In linear programming, shadow prices provide marginal values for right-hand sides. Their interpretation depends on constraint type: capacity constraints value extra processing; raw-material limits guide purchasing decisions; marketing bounds indicate cost of extra sales effort; quality stipulations show effect of tightening a specification (adjustment needed if the right-hand side coefficient involves a variable). Material-balance constraints with zero right-hand side often lack meaningful interpretation. Reduced costs measure the profit deficit for non-basic variables; basic variables have zero reduced cost (except when bounded).

The true marginal value for increasing a right-hand side is the minimum over all dual solutions; for decreasing, the maximum. Solvers output only one dual solution, which can mislead. Right-hand side ranges reveal validity: if a range extends only one side, the shadow price applies only to changes in that direction.

Gomory–Baumol cutting-plane-derived valuations are non-unique and may assign positive prices to non-negativity constraints even when the variable is positive, reflecting indivisibility cost. A duality gap remains.

To build stable models, replace a hard constraint \(\sum a_j x_j \le b\) with \(\sum a_j x_j - u = b\), where \(u\) is a new variable with a per-unit cost in the objective, allowing resource expansion at a price.

To convert product terms into separable form, replace \(x_1 x_2\) with new variables and constraints. One method defines \(u_1 = x_1 + x_2\), \(u_2 = x_1 - x_2\), then uses \(u_1^2 - u_2^2\) with equality constraints; the squares are separable and can be piecewise linearized, but mind whether \(u_2\) can be negative (use free variables or translate). Another method replaces the product with \(y\) and adds \(\log y = \log x_1 + \log x_2\); transform variables to avoid zero arguments to prevent \(-\infty\). Logarithms can cause numerical trouble if variables and their logs coexist in the model with widely different magnitudes.

Non-linear functions of a single variable are piecewise linearized via the \(\lambda\)-convention with convexity constraint \(\sum\lambda_i=1\) and the adjacency condition: at most two adjacent \(\lambda_i\) non-zero. This adjacency is enforced algorithmically by declaring \((\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)\) a Special Ordered Set of type 2 (SOS2). A Special Ordered Set of type 1 (SOS1) enforces that at most one variable in the set is non-zero, useful for selecting exactly one option among ordered alternatives (e.g., depot siting, capacity levels). SOS1 and SOS2 can be modeled with 0–1 variables: for SOS2, introduce binary \(\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{n-1}\) and constraints \(\lambda_1 \le \delta_1\), \(\lambda_2 \le \delta_1+\delta_2\), \(\lambda_3 \le \delta_2+\delta_3\), …, \(\lambda_n \le \delta_{n-1}\), plus \(\sum\delta_i =1\).

For non-separable functions of two variables \(g(x,y)\), define a grid with weights \(\lambda_{sk}\) and use row-wise sums \(\xi_s=\sum_k \lambda_{sk}\) and column-wise sums \(\eta_k=\sum_s \lambda_{sk}\). Declaring both \((\xi_1,\xi_2,\dots)\) and \((\eta_1,\eta_2,\dots)\) as SOS2 sets restricts non-zero \(\lambda_{sk}\) to at most four neighboring grid points. To force a unique representation (at most three points forming a triangle), add further diagonal SOS2 sets on \(\zeta_t = \sum_s \lambda_{s,t+s}\). When interpolation in one direction is not needed, keep grid-aligned values and avoid the row/column SOS2 overhead by using a chain of linked SOS sets.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary: Integer programming (IP) models discrete capacity expansion (integer variables for whole machines), logical conditions (binary variables with constraints like “if product A then B or C”), and combinatorial problems: sequencing (traveling salesman, job-shop scheduling), allocation, set partitioning (aircrew scheduling, assembly line balancing, cutting stock, political districting), quadratic assignment, resource-constrained PERT networks, and graph coloring. Decision variables are general integer or binary; objectives minimize cost, distance, or number of patterns. Constraints include logical implications, capacity limits, and set partitioning (each item assigned exactly once). Branch and bound, solving LP relaxations and branching on fractional variables, is the most practical MIP method; its success depends on formulation tightness. Use of cutting planes can strengthen relaxations. For cutting stock, column generation starts with a few patterns, solves the LP, and uses shadow prices to generate new patterns via a knapsack subproblem (solved efficiently by dynamic programming, not branch and bound). Set partitioning problems with enormous columns are handled similarly. Reformulating to tighten LP bounds, reducing integer variables, and exploiting problem structure improve solvability. Always test a small-scale version first. If too hard, use heuristics with good solutions as cut-off bounds in tree search. Avoid pure IP for resource-constrained PERT networks—heuristics are preferred due to computational intractability.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
In mixed-integer programming, 0–1 variables act as decisions (build/don’t build) or indicators linking continuous states. The constraint \(x - M\delta \le 0\) with large \(M\) forces \(\delta=1\) when \(x>0\), enabling fixed charges or conditional logic. In depot location, binary \(\delta_j\) for opening/expanding depots appear in capacity constraints: \(\sum_i x_{ij} \le T_j \delta_j\) blocks flow when closed. Expansion is modeled as \(\sum_i x_{i2} \le 50 + 20\delta_2\), where \(\delta_2=1\) grants 20 extra units. Cardinality limits like \(\sum_{j \notin \text{fixed}} \delta_j \le 2\) cap selected sites. Fixed costs enter the objective as linear terms \(10\delta_1 + 3\delta_2 + \dots\). Flow balance at depots equates total inflow and outflow; customer demand is met from factories and depots. A preference objective minimizes deviations by assigning cost 0 for preferred source and 1 otherwise, soft-constraining assignments.

Agricultural pricing uses revenue maximization \(\sum_i x_i p_i\) subject to fat/dry-matter resource limits and a price-index cap (linear regulatory constraint). Demand is linked to price via elasticity relations, requiring linearization of bilinear terms. Large distribution LPs can be solved with standard simplex, but specialized network algorithms offer compact solution of very large instances.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary: To impose logical conditions in optimization models, introduce 0–1 indicator variables \(\delta_i=1\) when proposition \(X_i\) holds. Basic connectives map to linear constraints: \(X_1 \lor X_2 \Rightarrow \delta_1+\delta_2 \ge 1\); \(X_1 \land X_2 \Rightarrow \delta_1=1,\delta_2=1\); \(\neg X_1 \Rightarrow \delta_1=0\); \(X_1 \rightarrow X_2 \Rightarrow \delta_1-\delta_2 \le 0\); \(X_1 \leftrightarrow X_2 \Rightarrow \delta_1-\delta_2=0\). Complex conditions use auxiliary binary variables that capture intermediate logical values. For example, \((X_A \lor X_B) \rightarrow (X_C \lor X_D \lor X_E)\) can be enforced by defining an auxiliary \(\delta\) equal to 1 if \(\delta_A+\delta_B\ge 1\), then requiring \(\delta=1 \Rightarrow \delta_C+\delta_D+\delta_E\ge 1\). This yields constraints \(\delta_A+\delta_B-2\delta \le 0\) and \(-\delta_C-\delta_D-\delta_E+\delta \le 0\). Boolean equivalences often produce tighter linear relaxations. Distributing implication over disjunction transforms the condition into \((X_A \rightarrow X_C\lor X_D\lor X_E) \land (X_B \rightarrow X_C\lor X_D\lor X_E)\), leading to \(\delta_A-\delta \le 0\), \(\delta_B-\delta \le 0\) and the same consequent constraint. The latter formulation is computationally preferable. Polynomial expressions like \(\delta_1\delta_2=0\) (mutual exclusion) linearize as \(\delta_1+\delta_2 \le 1\); more involved products can be linearized by introducing extra variables. All logical conditions thus reduce to linear inequalities over binary variables, and exploiting Boolean identities often improves model tightness.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
To model a piecewise linear function, introduce binary variables δ_k for each line segment and nonnegative weighting variables λ for breakpoints. Force exactly one segment active via sum δ_k = 1, with λ pairs linked to δ_k so only the active segment’s endpoints receive positive weight. The function’s input and output are convex combinations using those λ's.

Disjunctive constraints (at least one subset R_i must hold) are handled by indicator variables: δ_i = 1 → constraints in R_i satisfied, and sum δ_i ≥ 1. For “at least k out of N” subsets, sum δ_i ≥ k.

For a 0-1 knapsack constraint ∑ a_j δ_j ≤ a_0 with a_j ≥ 0, cover inequalities tighten the formulation. A cover is a set of indices whose coefficient sum exceeds a_0, implying not all can be 1: ∑_{i in cover} δ_i ≤ |cover| − 1. Minimal covers can be extended by adding variables with coefficients at least the largest in the cover, yielding stronger extended cover inequalities. The procedure of Balas generates facets with coefficients 0/±1.

A single 0-1 constraint can be simplified by re-expressing it in standard form with coefficients sorted descending, then identifying ceilings (maximal feasible subsets) and roofs (minimal infeasible subsets). Ceilings imply ∑ a_i ≤ a_0, roofs imply ∑ a_i ≥ a_0+1. Solving an LP over new coefficients a_i subject to these constraints plus ordering yields an equivalent simplified constraint.

In a combinatorial assignment problem (3D noughts and crosses), auxiliary binary variables γ_i represent whether a line is monochromatic. Constraints linking cell variables to γ_i enforce consistency; objective minimization of ∑ γ_i guarantees correct interpretation via optimality rather than explicit conditional logic.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
Vehicle routing problems (VRP) extend the TSP: a fleet of vehicles with capacities \(Q_k\) serves customers with demands \(q_i\), each visited by exactly one vehicle. Decision variables: binary arc selection \(\delta_{ijk}\) (vehicle \(k\) travels \(i\to j\)), visit indicator \(\gamma_{ik}\), and visit time \(\tau_i\). Constraints: \(\sum_k \gamma_{ik}=1\) for each customer; \(\sum_j \delta_{ijk} = \sum_j \delta_{jik} = \gamma_{ik}\); capacity \(\sum_i q_i \gamma_{ik} \le Q_k\); time propagation \(\tau_i - \tau_j \le M(1-\delta_{ijk}) - d_{ij}\); time windows \(a_i \le \tau_i \le b_i\). Objective minimizes cost \(\sum c_{ij}\delta_{ijk}\). Large instances are tackled by column generation: generate feasible routes (capacity + time windows) offline, then select and combine them in a master problem.

Quadratic assignment problems (QAP) assign \(n\) items to \(n\) positions with exactly one per position/row: \(\sum_j \delta_{ij}=1\), \(\sum_i \delta_{ij}=1\). units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
Integer programming formulations benefit more from structural tightening and meaningful branching variables than from minimizing variable count. The number of 0–1 variables is a poor proxy for computational difficulty because branch-and-bound often explores a negligible fraction of the potential tree.

A general non-negative integer variable γ with upper bound u can be expanded into 0–1 variables via γ = δ₀ + 2δ₁ + 4δ₂ + … + 2ʳδᵣ, where 2ʳ ≥ u. This adds roughly log₂ u binaries and is useful only when a 0–1-only algorithm requires it.

Introducing extra 0–1 variables that capture explicit dichotomies (e.g., location north/south, process batch/continuous) creates strong branching candidates. An integer slack variable in a constraint with integer coefficients and right-hand side, if prioritized for branching, acts as a cutting plane that tightens the LP relaxation.

Symmetry among indistinguishable entities (identical lorries, trips) produces redundant solutions across tree nodes. Aggregating such variables or imposing lexicographic ordering reduces this redundancy.

Big‑M coefficients should be as small as possible. Overly large M weakens the LP relaxation, permits spurious fractional solutions where δ is just below integer tolerance (e.g., x=5, δ=0.005 interpreted as integer), and introduces numerical instability. Splitting a single aggregated capacity constraint x₁+…+xₙ – Mδ ≤ 0 into individual constraints xᵢ – Mᵢδ ≤ 0 with Mᵢ tighter bounds the LP more strongly.

Disjunctive constraints of the form “at least one set Rₖ must hold” can be reformulated by splitting each variable xⱼ into components xⱼₖ per disjunct, imposing xⱼ = Σₖ xⱼₖ, Σₖ δₖ = 1, and constraints Σⱼ aᵢⱼₖ xⱼₖ – bᵢₖδₖ ≤ 0 for each disjunct. This requires closed feasible regions. Semi-continuous variables (x = 0 or x ≥ a) use x = a y₁ + M y₂, δ + y₁ + y₂ = 1, with δ binary and y₁,y₂ continuous, where M is a valid upper bound.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
Total unimodularity (TU) guarantees integer LP solutions for all integer right-hand sides. A sufficient condition (Property P) for TU: all entries are 0, ±1; each column has at most two nonzeros; rows can be partitioned into two sets such that columns with two same-sign entries have one in each set, and columns with opposite signs have both entries in the same set. The transpose case (each row has one +1 and one –1) also ensures TU.

A critical reformulation pattern: avoid aggregating logical constraints. The condition δ1 ∨ … ∨ δn → δ (all δ binary) is often written as δ1+…+δn – nδ ≤ 0. Disaggregating into n separate constraints δi – δ ≤ 0 yields a dual matrix that satisfies Property P and is totally unimodular. The aggregated form weakens the LP relaxation, admitting more fractional solutions; the disaggregated form tightens the relaxation and frequently makes branching unnecessary.

For big-M constraints linking binary indicators to continuous variables (e.g., x > 0 → δ = 1 modeled as x – Mδ ≤ 0), set M to the smallest valid upper bound on x. An overly large M enlarges the LP feasible region, hurting solvability. These patterns are directly transferable to UAV routing, facility location, and mission planning models where logical conditions and big-M links appear.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
Tightening integer programming models begins with bound strengthening: for each constraint, derive implied bounds on integer variables, then tighten to the nearest integer (e.g., for 0–1 variables, fix at 0 or 1). This alone can solve small problems.

A single 0–1 knapsack constraint can be simplified into an equivalent single constraint with smaller coefficients by solving an auxiliary LP; this produces the tightest single constraint without excluding integer solutions and reduces the LP feasible region. More powerful is expanding a single constraint into multiple constraints that define facets of the convex hull of feasible 0–1 points. Use minimal covers: given a ≤ constraint with nonnegative coefficients, a minimal cover is a set of indices whose coefficient sum exceeds the right-hand side. An extended cover adds indices whose coefficients are not smaller than any in the minimal cover. A strong cover yields a facet constraint of the form sum_{i in cover} δ_i ≤ r−1 where r is the cover size. All such constraints with 0/±1 coefficients can be systematically generated and appended to tighten the LP relaxation.

For logical constraints like “at most r customers supplied only if depot built,” the base constraint δ_1+…+δ_n ≤ r δ_{n+1} can be augmented with δ_i ≤ δ_{n+1} and the sum ≤ r−1+δ_{n+1}, obtained via strong covers after complementing δ_{n+1}. Appending these cuts can dramatically reduce branch-and-bound nodes. However, individual tightening of constraints does not guarantee the convex hull of the whole model; the LP may still be fractional. Convert general integer variables to binaries to apply these methods, but beware of size explosion.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
A reusable pattern for shared fixed-cost allocation: represent a network where arcs are revenue-generating activities that require both endpoint nodes (capital investments). Formulate a 0–1 IP with constraints like \(-δ_i + δ_{ij} \le 0\) linking arc selection to node usage. Solve the LP relaxation; the dual variables (shadow prices) of those linking constraints allocate node costs to incident arcs. Summing each node’s incoming allocation, prune any node whose total cannot cover its cost, yielding a maximum-profit subnetwork. No other cost division yields higher profit—a direct consequence of LP duality.

For mixed-integer programs (MIP), extracting economic marginal values from the LP subproblem at the optimal integer node is unreliable because integer variables change discretely. A somewhat more meaningful approach is to fix all integer variables at their optimal values, then perform sensitivity analysis on the remaining continuous part.

To avoid unrealistic discrete jumps in the optimal objective when right-hand sides change, introduce a continuous surplus variable with a penalty cost in the objective (and optionally a slack variable with its own cost). This makes the optimal objective a continuous, piecewise-linear function of the right-hand side and the solution semi-continuous—a vital stability modeling technique when budgets or capacities are not rigid.

For sensitivity analysis in IP, the only fully reliable method is re-solving with perturbed data, ideally warm-started from the previous solution. Always check if the constraint matrix is totally unimodular; if so, the problem can be solved as an LP, avoiding many of these difficulties.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
A corporate planning model maximizes total firm profit using a single centralized objective, which may require individual factories or departments to accept lower local profit than they would achieve if optimizing independently. This interdependence makes decentralized local optimization suboptimal in the presence of shared resources, capacity limits, or demand allocation; a monolithic multi-period linear program corrects it by simultaneously setting production, inventory, and transfer quantities across units.

A reusable pattern is a multi-plant, multi-period LP with rolling-horizon reruns each period: immediate operating decisions are implemented, while future periods remain provisional, updated with fresh forecasts. Include only variable costs in objective coefficients, standardize data from marketing (sales estimates), production (capacities, technological coefficients), and procurement (raw material costs). Maintain a central database compatible with the solver to feed regular reoptimization.

Decomposition is theoretically attractive to avoid a single enormous model but remains computationally unreliable for general use and often conflicts with acceptable organizational decentralization. Instead, use output filtering: a report writer isolates each department’s relevant portion of the solution to prevent information overload and to maintain acceptance.

Enable “what‑if” analysis via post‑optimal sensitivity ranges so managers can query scenarios without full reruns. Critical implementation caution: balance contact between model builders, data providers, and decision makers to prevent stale or misaligned inputs.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
Factory planning: multi-period production under machine maintenance. Machines must be down one month in six (grinders two of six). Binary variables per machine per month model maintenance flexibility, but this symmetric formulation creates equivalent alternate solutions, harming branch-and-bound. Use a feasible fixed-schedule solution as a cut-off. Inventory holding cost, finite storage capacity, and end-of-horizon stock targets apply alongside marketing limits per product per month.

Manpower planning: discrete-time LP for unskilled, semi-skilled, and skilled workers. Continuity constraints apply natural wastage rates (different for less than and more than one year of service) together with recruitment, retraining, downgrading (50% immediate additional wastage), redundancy, and short-time working (each short-time worker provides half a full-time equivalent). Retraining unskilled to semi-skilled is capped absolutely; semi-skilled to skilled is capped at 25% of the current skilled stock. Overmanning is limited to 150 total surplus workers across all skills; short-time is capped at 50 per skill. Two objectives—minimize total redundancies and minimize total cost—are reconciled by treating one as a constraint and performing parametric programming on its right-hand side, or by including both as non-constraint rows for multi-objective optimization within a single run. All adjustments are assumed to occur on the first day of each year.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
This LP refinery model captures blending and process selection with capacity limits, quality specifications, and fixed recipe constraints. The domain entities: two crudes, six distillation fractions (light/medium/heavy naphtha, light/heavy oil, residuum), reforming and cracking process units, and five final products (premium petrol, regular petrol, jet fuel, fuel oil, lube-oil). Decision variables measure each material flow along all possible processing and blending pathways (36 named variables). Objective is profit maximization (pence per barrel for each product).

Core constraints: crude availability and distillation capacity upper bounds; reforming and cracking capacity limits; lube-oil production within [500, 1000] barrels. Continuity constraints balance each fraction produced from crude distillation against its uses (reforming, cracking, blending, or fixed fuel-oil proportion). Process yields are linear: reforming gives 0.6, 0.52, 0.45 barrels reformed gasoline per barrel of light, medium, heavy naphtha; cracking yields cracked gasoline and cracked oil from light and heavy oil with fixed coefficients. Blending is linear by volume for octane and vapour pressure. Regular petrol octane ≥84, premium ≥94 constraints enforce quality via weighted sums of component octanes. Jet fuel vapour pressure constraint uses linear blending of components’ pressures (1.0, 0.6, 1.5, 0.05 kg/cm²) to not exceed 1 kg/cm². Fuel oil requires a fixed ratio of light oil, cracked oil, heavy oil, residuum as 10:4:3:1. Premium petrol production must be at least 40% of regular. This small LP (29 constraints, simple bounds) illustrates a pattern of linking yield, blending, and quality constraints with process selection; parametric programming on capacity right-hand sides is suggested for sensitivity analysis. Similar models scale to multi-refinery structured LPs.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
Dynamic multi-sector planning with production and capacity expansion can be modeled as a linear program using input-output time lags: current output requires inputs from the previous period (production coefficients) while new capacity requires inputs two periods earlier. State variables: output \(x_{it}\), start-of-period stock \(s_{it}\), and capacity additions \(y_{it}\) becoming effective in period \(t\). Material balance constraints link these with exogenous demand; manpower is a linear combination of outputs and capacity additions, subject to a global limit. Productive capacity bounds output by initial capacity plus cumulative past additions. To avoid end-of-horizon myopia, assume steady state beyond the planning window—solve a static Leontief model to derive terminal lower bounds on output and stock, forcing enough intermediate activity. Different policy goals are captured by swapping the objective (max terminal capacity, max late-horizon output, max manpower usage) and selectively relaxing constraints (e.g., ignoring demand or the manpower limit). This template transfers to any capacity-expansion problem with interdependent sectors.  

Facility location under interaction costs: departments \(i,k\) have communication volume \(C_{ik}\); site pairs \(j,l\) have unit cost \(D_{jl}\). Total communication cost is \(\sum C_{ik}D_{jl}X_{ij}X_{kl}\), linearizable for binary assignment variables with standard transformations. Each site has capacity (max departments). The resulting mixed-integer program is a quadratic assignment variant separable when \(D_{jl}\) decomposes.  

Curve fitting: minimizing sum of absolute deviations (L1) or maximum absolute deviation (Chebyshev) are linear programming problems using nonnegative deviation variables.

units.summary:
Airline yield management: three-class seats per plane (First 37, Business 38, Economy 47), up to six planes, £50k hire cost each, up to 10% seats transferable between adjacent classes. Multi-period stochastic program with recourse: decisions in period 1 set current price option (3 discrete options per class) and sales quantities, plus provisional price options for periods 2 and 3 contingent on demand scenarios. Objective maximizes expected revenue minus plane costs. Demand uncertain, three scenarios per period (probabilities 0.1,0.7,0.2), scenario-dependent demand varying by chosen price. Non-anticipativity: first-period decisions must be feasible for all subsequent scenario realizations; later periods can adapt after observing actual demand. Rolling-horizon re-optimization after each period using realized demands yields higher total yield than a single expected-value plan; topping-up last-period capacity further improves yield.

Car rental fleet management: multi-day rentals (1–3 days) with inter-depot returns, closed Sundays. Modeled as a time-space network flow: nodes for each depot-day, arcs for rentals of each duration and return location, tracking undamaged and damaged car inventories. Decision variables include fleet size and daily rental assignments. Demand may be partially satisfied; objective maximizes weekly profit.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
A multi-depot car rental network with four locations, two repair centers (Manchester 12, Birmingham 20 cars/day), and daily operations. Rental durations are 1–3 days with fixed aggregate proportions (55%/20%/25%); 10% of returns are damaged. Transfer of cars between depots takes one day; repair also takes one day. Rental demand varies by day and depot. Demand is capped but not all must be met; integrality of fleet count is relaxed.

Base model (LP) decides total fleet size and daily flows to maximize weekly profit under a steady-state assumption where the same expected stock repeats each week. The daily sequence is circular (Monday follows Saturday). Variables include undamaged/damaged inventories, rentals, transfers, and repairs per depot per day. Flow constraints capture multi-day returns: for each depot-day, undamaged arrivals sum over previous rental days’ returns (with return-to-depot proportions) plus arriving transfers plus repairs completed yesterday plus leftover. Damaged arrivals analogously use the 10% damaged fraction and include arriving damaged transfers. Outflow constraints allocate undamaged cars among rentals, outgoing transfers, and leftover, while damaged cars go to repair same-day or outgoing transfers or leftover. Repair capacity limits daily repair starts. A fleet-size consistency equation ties total cars to rentals in progress and all cars in depots on a chosen weekday. Profit includes rental revenue minus marginal costs, plus a £10 per rental expected surcharge from damage excesses, minus per-car weekly opportunity cost (£15) and transfer costs. Shadow prices on repair constraints are high (£617–646/day), indicating bottleneck.

Expansion decisions are modeled later with binary variables for adding 5-car blocks at specific depots. Precedence constraints require first expansion before second at same depot, and at most three total expansions. The MIP solves quickly (5 nodes) by augmenting the LP. The fleet count is treated as continuous, giving actionable rounded solutions.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
In urban air mobility and UAV logistics, linear programming models maximize profit contribution by setting flight frequencies or cargo volumes subject to capacity constraints on airspace sectors, vertiport slots, battery recharge availability, and fleet resources. Each capacity constraint’s shadow price is the marginal value of a small, single-resource increase, valid only within its right-hand-side range. For simultaneous expansions (e.g., adding landing slots and charging stations together), use parametric programming with a scaling parameter on the right-hand side.

Implement simple upper bounds (e.g., max landings per vertiport) as variable bounds, not explicit rows; the variable’s reduced cost then directly reflects the value of relaxing that bound. Reduced costs on inactive services indicate the objective coefficient improvement needed for them to become worthwhile. Never construct a dual manually—rely on solver output for shadow prices and ranges.

Degeneracy can produce multiple dual solutions, making a reported shadow price one of several; the true marginal value of an increase is the minimum over all dual solutions. A zero shadow price may still correspond to a binding constraint under alternative optima, so do not treat it as non-binding. Redundant constraints can distort ranging information; keep formulations parsimonious. For integer programs, LP-style shadow prices fail—slack resources can carry value, and valuations are non-unique. To stabilize models, replace hard constraints with soft versions by adding a slack variable costed in the objective, enabling resource expansion at a chosen price. Right-hand-side ranges and marginal rates of substitution describe how optimal mixes shift, guiding infrastructure decisions under single-parameter changes.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
Linearizing a minimax objective: introduce variable \(z\) and constraints \(\sum_j a_{ij}x_j - z \le 0\), minimize \(z\). For ratio objectives \(\max (\sum a_j x_j)/(\sum b_j x_j)\) with denominator always nonzero and of constant sign, use the Charnes‑Cooper transformation: set \(t = 1/(\sum b_j x_j)\), define \(w_j = t x_j\), maximize \(\sum a_j w_j\) subject to \(\sum b_j w_j = 1\), transform each original constraint \(\sum d_j x_j\,(\le,=,\ge)\,e\) into \(\sum d_j w_j - e t\,(\le,=,\ge)\,0\), and recover \(x_j = w_j/t\) (reverse inequalities if denominator negative). Chance constraints \(P[\sum a_j x_j \le b] \ge \beta\) become a deterministic bound \(b'\) that ensures the required probability.

Goal programming softens hard equations \(\sum a_{ij}x_j = b_i\) into \(\sum a_{ij}x_j + u_i - v_i = b_i\) with \(u_i,v_i\ge 0\), minimizing either the weighted sum of deviations or the maximum deviation (\(\min z\) with \(z \ge u_i, z \ge v_i\)). The minimax deviation form directly applies to curve fitting. Binary quadratic terms \(\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}\) are made linear via new binary \(\gamma_{ijkl}\) and constraints \(\gamma_{ijkl} \le \delta_{ij}\), \(\gamma_{ijkl} \le \delta_{kl}\), \(\delta_{ij}+\delta_{kl}-\gamma_{ijkl} \le 1\). When a compact formulation yields a weak LP relaxation, selectively expanding some constraints before branching improves bounds; assignment constraints often form special ordered sets of type 1.

Two‑stage stochastic recourse with discrete scenarios: first‑stage variables \(x_j\); for each scenario \(r\) (probability \(p_r\)) define recourse variables \(y_j^{(r)}\) (excess) and \(z_j^{(r)}\) (shortfall) satisfying \(x_j - y_j^{(r)} + z_j^{(r)} = d_j^{(r)}\). Objective minimizes \(\sum c_j x_j + \sum_r p_r (\sum e_j y_j^{(r)} + f_j z_j^{(r)})\). The LP matrix is block‑angular, enabling Benders decomposition. Scenario trees multiply with stages; reduce scenarios or decouple. Alternative risk attitudes are captured by maximin or chance‑constrained objectives.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
Soft constraints are created by adding a non‑negative slack variable \(u\) to a hard limit \(\sum a_j x_j \le b\) and penalizing \(u\) in the objective; equality constraints require a pair \((u,v)\) with separate penalties, and at most one is positive at optimum. For binary‑driven implications, \(\delta=1 \Rightarrow \sum a_j x_j \le b\) is enforced by \(\sum a_j x_j + M\delta \le M+b\) with \(M\) a tight upper bound on the excess. The reverse implication uses a small tolerance \(\varepsilon\) (1 for integers) and a tight lower bound \(m\): \(\delta=0 \Rightarrow \sum a_j x_j \ge b+\varepsilon\) becomes \(\sum a_j x_j - (m-\varepsilon)\delta \ge b+\varepsilon\). These patterns transfer directly to air mobility: soft vertiport slot limits penalizing over‑scheduling; conditional activation of air corridors or charging stations linked to facility‑opening binaries; and depot‑delivery relations where no deliveries originate if a depot is not opened.

Model construction must use explicit, mnemonic variables rather than implicit substitutions to ease debugging. Infeasibility is checked by inserting a known feasible point (a past schedule) to detect over‑restrictive constraints. Unboundedness often signals missing material‑balance or capacity constraints; the intermediate solution printed before termination reveals physically impossible activities. Hard constraints can be softened temporarily to prevent artificial infeasibility and expose violation magnitudes. Validate a solvable model by optimizing several contrived objectives to stress‑test subsets of constraints, exposing missing restrictions iteratively. Keep big‑\(M\) and small‑\(m\) values as tight as possible to improve solver performance.

units.title: Model Building in Mathematical Programming
units.summary:
Corporate planning models with multiple factories sharing a scarce resource (e.g., raw material) exhibit a block-angular LP structure: a common row couples plant-specific capacity submodels. Decision variables are production quantities per product per plant. The objective maximizes total profit across all units; constraints include shared raw material supply, local grinding/polishing hours, and product-to-plant assignments.

Decomposition via Dantzig-Wolfe treats each plant as a subproblem generating extreme-point production proposals. The master problem selects convex combinations of these proposals (weights summing to 1 per plant) subject only to the common resource constraint. The master’s shadow price becomes an internal transfer price charged to subproblems, which re-optimize their local profit minus resource cost to generate new columns. Iteration stops when no favorable reduced-cost proposal remains. Unbounded subproblem feasible regions require generating extreme rays for correct pricing.

Despite its theoretical appeal, decomposition often proves computationally unreliable in practice. A preferred alternative is a monolithic multi-period LP with rolling-horizon reruns: immediate decisions are implemented, future periods re-optimized with updated forecasts. Only variable costs appear in the objective. Output filtering isolates each department’s relevant actions, preserving acceptance without actual organizational decentralization. For multi-period models, staircase structures can be converted to block-angular; common-column structures (dual) allow Benders decomposition. Stochastic extensions use scenario trees with shared first-stage variables.

Implementation cautions: maintain a central solver-compatible database; balance frequent contact among model builders, data providers, and decision makers to avoid stale inputs; use post-optimal sensitivity ranges for “what-if” analysis rather than full reruns.

units.title: A Comprehensive Review of Building the Resilience of Low-Altitude Logistics: Key Issues, Challenges, and Strategies
units.summary: Low‑altitude logistics resilience decomposes into robustness, adaptability, recoverability, and redundancy, each imposing distinct modeling requirements. Robustness calls for solutions that remain feasible under perturbations; typical models use uncertainty sets on wind impact, battery discharge rates, and travel times, enforced via robust or distributionally robust constraints on payload‑energy budgets. Adaptability maps to two‑stage stochastic or online optimization with recourse, where first‑stage routing and charging decisions are updated after real‑time wind, UTM clearance, and cyber‑threat observations; recourse decisions re‑route or delay flights within dynamically reconfigured airspace sectors. Recoverability is captured by a recovery‑time objective (RTO): after a disruption (e.g., a lost drone, infrastructure outage), idle UAVs and backup charging stations are re‑deployed to minimize cumulative downtime, often solved as a shortest‑restoration scheduling problem. Redundancy is modeled by a surplus budget: spare drones, batteries, and alternate landing pads are pre‑positioned, treated as decision variables that satisfy coverage constraints while ensuring a minimum backup capacity ratio. Airspace capacity and UTM sector limits act as simultaneous flight count constraints; regulatory sandboxes relax these bounds during trial periods. Hard constraints include battery energy density dictating feasible range, payload mass limits, and safety thresholds from performance‑based regulation (e.g., maximum allowable failure probability under weather). Solution methods include AI‑driven risk‑aware planning (deep RL for adaptive routing), digital‑twin simulation for scenario generation, and Benders‑based decomposition for two‑stage models with recovery subproblems.

units.title: Adaptive airspace allocation model for urban drone logistics using multi-objective optimization under uncertainty
units.summary:
Urban UAV logistics airspace allocation is modeled as a dynamic resource allocation problem in a 3D airspace with an octree index (query complexity O(log n)). Decision variables involve spatial route/cell assignments for multiple UAVs under three competing objectives: delivery time, conflict risk (safety), and operating cost. The multi-objective formulation seeks a Pareto front approximation subject to safety-margin constraints.

Uncertainty stems from demand fluctuations, meteorological variations, and emergency scenarios, with explicit cross-factor interaction mechanisms. The robustness model uses a Wasserstein distributionally robust set D = {P : W_p(P, P0) ≤ ε} around an empirical distribution P0. The resulting min-max objective min_X max_{P∈D} E_P[F(X,ξ)] is dualized to min_{X,λ} λε + E_{P0}[ sup( F(X,ξ) − λ‖ξ−ξ0‖^p ) ], enabling tractable alternating optimization.

A two-tier hybrid architecture couples a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) policy (attention-enhanced, with a 10,000-capacity experience replay pool) for real-time decisions and a lower-level DRO routine that supplies worst-case guarantees, adaptively linked via the confidence parameter ε. The DRL policy gradient converges at O(1/√T) under Robbins-Monro conditions. Pareto-optimality is characterized by KKT conditions Σ λ_i ∇f_i + Σ μ_j ∇g_j = 0 with weights λ_i ≥ 0 summing to one. The improved MOEA/D-DRL algorithm applies Chebyshev decomposition to generate N parallel scalar subproblems, uses spherical vector coding for high-dimensional search, and prunes invalid configurations, achieving an overall O(n log n) complexity. The method produces a full Pareto set in which all candidates satisfy safety constraints. Implementation notes: 1,000 flights are processed in 4.7 seconds; edge computing can offload central nodes; communication bandwidth and millisecond-level decision latency remain limiting factors.

units.title: Drone-aided routing: A literature review
units.summary:
Domain entities include distribution centers, drones, and ground vehicles (trucks, vans). Real configurations: Zipline’s multi-depot network delivering vaccines and blood directly to health facilities; Mercedes-Benz’s Vision Van acting as a moving drone launch platform for last-mile e-commerce delivery.

Core problem classes are the Traveling Salesman Problem with Drone (TSP-D) and Vehicle Routing Problem with Drone (VRP-D). Decision variables: assignment of customers to drone or truck, routing sequences, and synchronization points/times where a drone launches from and lands back on the truck. Key constraints: drone battery range limiting flight distance, payload capacity (often one small parcel), truck capacity, and temporal coordination ensuring the drone rendezvous before battery depletion. Objectives: minimize makespan (total delivery time) or total operational cost (energy, fixed vehicle expenses). Variants also include drone-only direct deliveries from a depot under range limits.

Solution methods span exact branch-and-price and branch-and-cut, alongside metaheuristics like adaptive large neighborhood search. Classification taxonomies use attributes such as problem objective, constraint types, solution approach, and whether a complementary ground vehicle is employed. The literature is predominantly deterministic; battery consumption is typically encoded as a maximum distance constraint, and no airspace regulations or uncertainty are modeled.

units.title: Drone-aided routing: A literature review
units.summary: Drone routing problems involve aerial vehicles with limited payload capacity and flight endurance dictated by battery life. Energy consumption is influenced by drone type (e.g., wing-rotary configurations incur higher routing cost) and is uncertain due to weather and atmospheric temperature. Safety regulations impose hard constraints: maximum allowable altitude, prohibited night operations, no-fly zones, and per-drone load limits. In humanitarian facility location, a stochastic model treats drone battery life as an uncertain operating condition and uses a fast heuristic algorithm. Dynamic combined truck-and-drone delivery problems model a drone that resupplies a truck in real time as customer requests arrive, requiring efficient online algorithms. Objectives typically trade off speed against energy and operating cost. Key constraints to embed in any drone routing model are battery capacity, payload limits, weather-dependent energy usage, regulatory time windows (daylight only), and geofencing exclusions. Uncertainty sources include travel times, demands, and energy availability from temperature. Realistic modeling must integrate these technological limits and local airspace rules.

units.title: Drone-aided routing: A literature review
units.summary: Drone-selection attributes for routing models derive from fuselage type and propulsion. Fixed-wing UAVs offer lower energy consumption, long range, and high payload capacity but cannot hover, restricting them to line-haul tasks. Rotary-wing platforms (quadcopters, hexacopters) enable vertical take-off/landing and precise hovering, required for monitoring or delivery to constrained sites, at the cost of higher energy consumption and maintenance complexity. Flapping-wing designs achieve unique maneuverability at micro-air-vehicle scales. Propulsion systems impose operational constraints: battery-based electric motors (brushless, lithium cells) are silent, lightweight, and low-maintenance but suffer limited endurance and recharge cycles, making routing dependent on charging/swapping location and time windows. Gas turbines provide higher power density and longer endurance but with greater weight, cost, and noise. These features become model parameters for each drone class: maximal payload, cruise and hover power, maximum range, VTOL capability (binary), and maintenance-cost coefficient. A task requiring stationary observation forces drone assignment to rotary-wing/hybrid types. Energy-limited battery drones introduce range constraints and the need to integrate recharging nodes into route planning. Objectives can incorporate type-dependent acquisition, energy, and maintenance costs. Safety levels (reported as high for fixed-wing, medium for rotary, low for flapping) may enter risk constraints.

units.title: Drone-aided routing: A literature review
units.summary:
The core entities are a depot, trucks (carriers, sometimes capacity-constrained), drones (payload-limited, battery-autonomy-constrained, possibly with different speeds), and customers (some truck-only). The literature classifies problems into two macro-classes: deliveries by either trucks or drones (TSP-D, VRP-D) and deliveries only by drones (DDP, CVP-D). In FSTSP (single truck, single drone, tandem operations), a drone may launch and retrieve at nodes or any point on an arc, visit one or multiple customers, and must respect flight endurance; the truck may wait or not. Objectives include makespan, completion time, total operational cost (transportation plus waiting time), and customer waiting time. PDSTSP uses independent truck and multiple drones with multi-trip depot-based sorties. VRP-D generalizes to multiple trucks with multiple drones, adding capacity, cyclic operations, and en-route launch/collect points. CVP-D assumes a fixed truck route and schedules drone deliveries from it.

Constraints: drone energy consumption modeled as linear in distance or as function of parcel weight, speed, and operation time (eight flight phases); battery swap/recharge; no-fly zones; payload restrictions; synchronization (truck must retrieve drone at same or later stop). A recurring insight: drone speed must be at least twice truck speed for significant time savings. Allowing launch/retrieve points anywhere on arcs rather than only at customer nodes yields substantial improvements. Deterministic settings dominate; very few stochastic/dynamic models exist. Method patterns: route-first cluster-second (solve TSP, then insert drone via heuristics); K-means clustering to select launch foci; metaheuristics (genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, GRASP, VNS); exact methods limited to about 30 customers for TSP-D due to complexity. Decompositions often separate truck routing and drone scheduling. Caution: modeling drone energy linearly with distance is common but some works use more detailed functions incorporating weight, speed, and flight phases, which impacts feasibility.

units.title: Drone-aided routing: A literature review
units.summary:
In drone-aided routing, core problem classes include the Flying Sidekick TSP (one truck, one drone, synchronization at rendezvous), Parallel Drone Scheduling TSP (multiple drones making multi-stop trips from a depot), two-echelon VRP‑D (trucks first level, drones second), drone‑only delivery with energy constraints, and carrier‑vehicle problems where a truck/aircraft acts as a mobile depot with a fixed or flexible route. Decisions typically involve customer‑to‑vehicle assignment, routing, launch/rendezvous timing, drone station location, and occasionally drone speed. Common objectives minimize completion time, makespan, operational cost, or total energy; multi‑objective forms balance cost, efficiency, and fleet size.

Constraints include drone endurance (battery capacity often a function of payload weight), payload limits, time windows, synchronization between drone and truck, and a limited number of drones per carrier. Drone recharge is sometimes considered, but charging time is frequently ignored; drone speed is often fixed because speed shows little cost impact under constant‑energy models. Station location adds fixed costs and capacity considerations.

Exact MILP models are solvable only for very small instances (≤11 customers). Decomposition approaches separate customer assignment and routing; matheuristics combine Lin‑Kernighan with local search or MILP. Dynamic variants handle resupply or stochastic demand, with drones replenishing moving trucks. A key domain rule: drone endurance and payload capacity strongly affect solution quality, while speed choice often does not, guiding model simplifications.

units.summary: Most TSP-D and VRP-D formulations assume a single truck with unlimited capacity and one or more drones. Drones typically perform a single delivery per sortie, often without capacity limits, energy models, or time windows. No surveyed work simultaneously considers customer time windows and drop-pickup operations. Common objectives are makespan minimization and transportation cost reduction. Realistic drone properties—rotor count, flight endurance, payload, speed, battery specifications, energy cost coefficients—are rarely incorporated, though they affect range and recharging needs. Key modeling gaps include: energy consumption and CO2 emissions, stochastic or dynamic requests, uncertain travel times and energy usage, drone station placement, and multiple-drone sorties with recharge planning. Synchronization constraints between truck and drone are typically deterministic. The literature lacks accurate energy models, so drone endurance is often a simple distance limit rather than a function of payload and battery state. For new tasks, reusable patterns include enforcing a single-drop-per-launch constraint, using makespan or cost objectives, and treating truck capacity as uncapacitated. Future models should incorporate payload-dependent energy consumption, recharge decisions, time windows, stochastic demand, and multiple drone deliveries per sortie.

units.title: Drone-aided routing: A literature review
units.summary:
For vehicle-drone routing problems (VRP-D), a common decomposition heuristic separates customer allocation (via savings heuristic and local search) from drone assignment (solved as a MILP). A recurring configuration: each truck carries one drone; the drone makes a single delivery, then re-joins the truck at a different point while the truck performs other deliveries.

CO₂ emission models for trucks are formulated as a function of distance travelled and total weight carried (including curb weight, drone weight aboard, and parcel weight). Drone emissions are treated as zero at the point of use but indirect emissions from electricity generation are considered. Objective functions studied include minimizing CO₂ and minimizing total cost (fuel + other). These models allow comparing pure-truck, truck-and-drone, and pure-drone fleet configurations.

Energy consumption for drones is typically abstracted as a maximum flight time or distance, with battery recharging assumed instantaneous. Incorporation of accurate energy models, intermediate recharging points, and partial battery depletion constraints is identified as an open gap, especially for VRP-D and TSP-D variants. Transshipment depots as drone parking/recharging bases and the use of alternative-fuel trucks are suggested extensions.

Key constraints: drone assigned to a single vehicle, drone must return to the same vehicle after a delivery (synchronized), and the launch and recovery nodes can differ. Solution methods include genetic algorithms and matheuristics combining routing heuristics with MILP assignment subproblems.

units.summary:

Fixed-wing types lack hover, restricting them to line-haul; rotary-wing/hybrid types are mandatory for tasks requiring stationary observation or delivery to constrained sites, with higher energy consumption. Propulsion type dictates endurance and recharging dependencies: battery-electric drones impose range constraints and require the insertion of charging/swapping nodes with time windows into routes; gas-turbine drones yield longer endurance but greater weight, cost, and noise.

Decision variables include fleet composition (type assignment) and task routes. Assignment feasibility is governed by binary capability matching: a task’s required hover capability forces a VTOL-capable type. Battery energy constraints translate to consumption budgets composed of cruise and hover power integrated over arcs, with recharge events at dedicated nodes. Objectives can incorporate type-dependent acquisition, energy, and maintenance costs. Safety risk levels (reported qualitatively as high/medium/low) can be embedded as risk constraints, for example capping the use of lower-safety types on certain tasks. The modeling pattern generalizes to heterogeneous vehicle routing with capability-constrained task allocation and energy-refueling logic.

units.title: Efficiency of UAV-based last-mile delivery under congestion in low-altitude air
units.summary: The study presents a steady-state continuous user equilibrium model for drone traffic in low-altitude 3D airspace during last-mile delivery. The domain Ω⊂ℝ³ is bounded, with inflow boundary Γin (customer locations) and exit boundary Γout (launching site). A time-invariant inflow rate q(x) enters at Γin. Local travel cost per unit distance c(x,‖f‖) is a non-decreasing function of flux magnitude ‖f‖, inducing congestion. Under Wardrop equilibrium, a potential function u(x) (minimum cost to reach exit) and divergence-free flux field f satisfy the coupled PDEs: ∇u = −c·(f/‖f‖) (Eikonal) and ∇·f = 0 (continuity), with boundary conditions f·n = q on Γin, u = u0 on Γout, and zero normal flux elsewhere. Solution uses a finite element scheme with Taylor-Hood element pairs to discretize and solve these equations directly. The model evaluates performance (travel time, energy consumption, drone density) for two facility configurations: a ground depot and an airborne fulfillment center (AFC) at varying hover heights. Sensitivity analysis reveals that higher AFC altitude (e.g., 700m) significantly reduces drone energy use and peak density compared to lower heights or ground-based systems. The approach captures trade-offs between delivery time and energy efficiency. Limitations include the single-commodity assumption; extensions to multi-commodity flows (multiple carriers or asymmetric inbound/outbound paths) and dynamic models with kinematic/density constraints for collision avoidance are noted. The equilibrium framework serves as a building block to optimize service areas or evaluate hybrid truck-drone coordination.

units.title: Efficiency of UAV-based last-mile delivery under congestion in low-altitude air
units.summary: UAV last-mile delivery congestion can be modeled macroscopically using continuum pedestrian flow analogues. Drone traffic is treated as a 2-D continuum satisfying flow conservation (continuity equation) and user equilibrium (Eikonal equation) where local travel cost increases with density. The flux field follows the steepest descent of a minimum-time potential penalized by congestion. With uniform outflow at delivery exits, boundary conditions become Neumann-type, reducing to a Poisson-like problem. This PDE system reveals density patterns and throughput limits, enabling capacity assessment. Analytical solutions exist for linear congestion cost functions; finite-element methods can handle general cases. The framework extends to facility location design (charging/launching station placement) under continuous traffic equilibrium, and to topological optimization of low-altitude guideways that detour traffic to relieve bottlenecks. At the operational level, drone routing is cast as a vehicle routing problem with battery recharging constraints, and coupled fleet/charging network operations can be optimized via dynamic pricing to manage time-varying demand and congestion. Real-time cloud-based navigation can implement system-optimal or user-equilibrium routing adjustments. Uncertainty from demand fluctuations and drone reliability can be incorporated through stochastic scheduling and reliability constraints upon these models.

units.summary: Traffic in a 2D airspace region Ω is represented by a flux field f(x) and a cost potential u(x). UAVs enter via inflow boundary Γ_in and converge to a single destination on outflow boundary Γ_out. Travel cost follows a BPR‑type congestion function c(x,‖f‖)=α(x)+β(x)‖f‖^γ(x) with α the free‑flow reciprocal speed. Drone density ρ(x)=α‖f‖+β‖f‖^γ⁺¹ emerges from the speed–flow relation; a safety cap ρ(x)≤ρ0 imposes a mass‑conservation limit on total inflow: ∫_Γin q dx must not exceed the outflow capacity otherwise density is violated. User equilibrium is described by (f/‖f‖)c+∇u=0 and ∇·f=q on Γ_in, with u prescribed on Γ_out. For system optimum, replace c by c+‖f‖∂c/∂‖f‖. The mixed weak form is discretized with Taylor–Hood finite elements (vector flux Pd+1, scalar potential Pd) and solved by Newton’s method, linearizing the residual via Gateaux derivatives. Verification traces path lines from the velocity field and checks consistency with Dijkstra shortest paths on the mesh. Practical cautions: the BPR function may need piecewise handling in highly congested regimes; additional kinematic bounds (e.g., acceleration) can be layered on. The continuum PDE framework generalises to coordinated multi‑provider airspace sharing via marginal‑cost pricing.

units.title: Efficiency of UAV-based last-mile delivery under congestion in low-altitude air
units.summary:
The model describes UAV last-mile delivery in 3D airspace as a continuum traffic equilibrium problem. The domain is a hemisphere or cylinder with an origin depot (ground or airborne) and a customer area on the ground; drones enter from an inlet boundary and exit through an outlet boundary. Virtual barriers (buildings) restrict low-altitude flight.

State variables are flux vector **v**(x) and scalar cost potential φ(x). Conservation of flow: ∇·**v** = q (demand rate). Travel cost per unit distance is congestion-dependent: c(x,|**v**|)=α(x)+β(x)|**v**|^γ. The equilibrium minimizes total travel time (free-flow plus delay); the optimality condition yields **v** parallel to ∇φ and a nonlinear relation between |**v**| and |∇φ|, reducing to a nonlinear Poisson equation for φ.

Decision variables include barrier geometry (opening ratio, height) and airship hovering altitude. Objective: minimize average total travel time or energy consumption. Energy consumption uses mode-specific powers (hover 660 W with payload, ascend 720 W, descend 0 W, idle 260 W) scaled by time spent in each state. Constraints: no-fly zones are impermeable or incur infinite cost; mesh boundaries require smooth resolution.

Numerical solution uses the finite element method (Taylor–Hood elements, P3/P2) with Newton iteration; linearized systems are solved via Krylov methods (PETSc). A good initial guess comes from the linear problem (α=0, β=1) which becomes a Poisson equation. Mesh refinement adds inflation layers near boundaries to capture sharp flux changes. Caution: Newton may not converge to global optimum due to non-convex residual.

Key insights: Restricting near-ground flight (e.g., full blockage with a low barrier) can reduce total travel time by dispersing congestion—a Braess-like paradox. For airborne fulfillment centers, lower hovering height (~500 m) minimizes travel time, but energy tradeoffs depend on ascent costs. The model can be transferred to design airspace structures and no-fly zones.

units.title: Optimization approaches for civil applications of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) or aerial drones: A survey
units.summary:
Search problems use cell‑based probability maps with detection probability π < 1 per visit, often varying per cell due to line‑of‑sight obstacles and sensor footprint shape. Decision problems maximize cumulative detection probability within a time limit, or minimize time to reach a target confidence; optimal paths need not traverse the highest‑probability cell because detection accumulates along the route. An alternative formulation labels cells with information uncertainty indices that decrease by a constant factor after each drone visit, with the objective of maximizing total uncertainty reduction.

Key constraints: limited flight endurance requiring depot refueling (biasing search intensity toward the depot), gliding drones that exploit thermals, restricted communication between drones forcing explicit information‑exchange limits, and strategic interactions when drones belong to different entities (selfish, cooperative, or adversarial). When drones must also estimate motion parameters of moving objects (e.g., icebergs), the problem becomes a graph‑theoretic assignment and routing task: objects with highest observational uncertainty are visited first. Cyclic‑routing models address periodic updates of object positions. For coverage with unknown obstacles, a drone must predict obstacle motion to maximize covered area within flight time while avoiding collisions.

Solution patterns: integrate control frameworks for joint estimation and path planning, graph‑based assignment with prioritized visits according to uncertainty, and constant‑factor uncertainty‑reduction heuristics.

units.title: Optimization approaches for civil applications of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) or aerial drones: A survey
units.summary: This survey distills UAV communication modeling patterns. Key entities: drones (as flying base stations, data collectors, or relays), ground control stations, users/sensors, and FANET nodes. Decision variables include drone positions/trajectories, assignment of time-frequency slots (TDMA, FDMA), relay placement, data collection sequences, and transmission power. Constraints arise from: probabilistic line-of-sight (LoS) dependent on building density, altitude, and distance; path loss models (free-space or log-distance); fading distributions (Rayleigh for urban, Rician if LoS dominant, Nakagami-m); SNR thresholds for successful links; limited communication range; interference from other links; finite onboard memory/buffer for sensor data; energy budgets that sum propulsion and transmission (often proportional to data volume and distance); and kinematic limits (minimum turning radius, smooth Bezier curves, max speed, wind uncertainty). Typical objectives minimize energy, maximize number of served links or coverage probability, or minimize packet delay. Drone-to-drone relaying extends range, speeds up multi-hop message delivery, and frees buffers; GPS-denied areas are served by relay drones. Models use mixed-integer programming, dynamic programming, game theory, and chance constraints for fading. Lagrangian relaxation, branch-and-bound, heuristics, and experimental validation appear as solution methods. A reusable pattern penalizes or avoids paths through signal-shadowed zones (behind buildings, under tree crowns) in path planning.
