units.title: Optimization approaches for civil applications of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) or aerial drones: A survey
units.summary:
Coverage path planning (CPP) minimizes path length, completion time, or energy consumption (altitude/acceleration-dependent). Turning costs make number of turns a proxy objective; lawnmower patterns minimize turns by aligning the sweep direction with the smallest width of a convex area. Terrain elevation significantly alters optimal paths; ignoring it multiplies length and energy. Exact CPP uses analytic geometry; discretizing area into a grid converts it to a routing problem but is only a heuristic.

Routing with minimum turning radius yields Dubins paths: straight segments and turns at the minimum radius. Dubins TSP/VRP is NP-hard. Heuristics solve Euclidean TSP then adjust paths, or randomly assign headings and solve an asymmetric TSP. The k-neighbor TSP makes tour length depend on edge sequences. Neighborhood routing (visiting exactly one point per region) models sensor footprints or spatial correlation, introducing one-in-a-set constraints.

Limited range requires depot recharging and battery size selection (weight vs. energy tradeoff). Shared airspace deconfliction formulates a time-dependent TSP with ascent/descent angles, solved via mixed-integer programming with valid cuts. Disaster facility location places transfer centers using drones and off-road vehicles, considering damaged road edges and loading/unloading times. Game-theoretic models handle adversarial attacks as zero-sum games on graphs with node attack success probabilities. Additional constraints: soft time windows, angle/height requirements for imaging, and sensor-specific drone eligibility.

UAV partial coverage problems with budget limits (time, energy) require selecting which region nodes to visit to maximize collected information value. The area P is discretized into a graph where nodes carry rewards or importance scores. This directly yields an orienteering problem: given a travel budget, maximize total reward from visited nodes while respecting origin–destination constraints.

Decision variables: node visit sequencing; optional detours to capture detected anomalies with associated rewards. Objectives: maximize value of collected information; or minimize information delay (time from capture to processing unit). Constraints: energy/time budgets, forbidden regions (handled via penalties or hard exclusion), and queuing delays if a human operator must launch/relaunch each drone. Penalties for distance traveled, energy expenditure, and forbidden region incursion are often incorporated into the objective.

Multiple independent drones can negotiate area partitioning through auction protocols to allocate responsibilities. Operator availability acts as a capacitated shared resource, introducing waiting times that delay task completion. The orienteering model extends to continuous motion with different sensor detection ranges and can be solved with standard routing metaheuristics; implementing it requires careful discretization of detection footprints into reward-bearing nodes.

units.summary: Drones may be heterogeneous (speed, payload, layer) and operate in airspace with vertical displacement points for package exchange, recharging stations, or highways as mandated flight corridors. Coverage tasks demand loitering with handover when battery is insufficient. Relevant problems: orienteering with time windows and uncertain incident rewards (probability-weighted), multi-objective routing balancing information value and flight time, task assignment minimizing makespan when service times dominate travel, data gathering under communication range, memory, and recency constraints, and WSN lifetime maximization (time until first sensor energy depletion) via sink reassignment. A common pattern is hierarchical decomposition: cluster sensors first, then route over cluster heads. When processing times greatly exceed travel, routing approximates scheduling. Trade-offs appear between collecting extra network state information and delay, and between reward value and flying time.

units.summary: In UAV communication relay and cloudlet problems, drones serve as aerial base stations or relays. Decision variables include stationary placement coordinates and altitude, flight trajectories (cyclic paths or hover pauses), time-slot assignments to ground users under TDMA, transmission power allocation among source and relay drones, and beaconing interval start/duration for user discovery. Objectives: maximize radio coverage or coverage probability, minimize total energy expenditure (propulsion plus communication). Key constraints: nonlinear SINR thresholds, device-to-device interference, flight dynamics (e.g., fixed-wing propulsion power dominates communication power), and user location distributions (known or random). Uncertainty arises from random user densities and moving nodes. Analytic formulas can determine optimal altitude given horizontal position to maximize coverage, and coverage probability under distributional assumptions. Trajectory optimization must jointly model propulsion energy and communication scheduling; neglecting propulsion leads to poor strategies because hovering/flight energy far exceeds transmission energy. Multi-hop drone networks add relay power allocation constraints. Competitive providers lead to game-theoretic formulations: drones choose beaconing interval parameters to maximize connection probability with passively scanning users. Implementation insight: always couple the energy-intensive flight model with communication decisions.

units.summary: Combined operations pair drones (limited endurance, often one-package-per-sortie) with ground vehicles that serve as carriers, recharging platforms, or independent delivery units. When sync is absent, the drone visitation task on a UGV reduces to an orienteering problem; drone-truck delivery without waiting transforms into an asymmetric TSP. With synchronization, the flying-sidekick TSP (TSP-D) forces drone launch/recovery only at truck-served customer stops, introducing waiting costs; extensions include the VRP with drones and cross-docking choices. Independent deliveries from a depot minimize makespan by jointly determining fleet sizes and tours, while same-day order acceptance selects drone or truck modes. Solution approaches include continuous approximation (L1/L2 metrics) to derive expected cost/time formulas, worst-case bounds analogous to Amdahl’s law (a single drone per truck can halve delivery time), and connections to min–max and close-enough VRP. Heterogeneous observational resources (drones, airships, satellites) are assigned tasks considering each unit’s strengths and constraints.

units.summary: UAM modeling focuses on short-range, low-altitude eVTOL operations with limited passenger capacity. Core decision variables include vehicle routing, repositioning flows (especially airport shuttle networks where fixed routes connect 1–2 major airports to designated urban vertiports), and vertiport location. Repositioning is needed to balance supply with asymmetric demand. Commuting networks exhibit high peak-hour volumes; capacity constraints and time-of-day pricing become critical. Vertiport capacity can use existing rooftop sites, reducing new construction. Emergency medical services introduce unpredictable demand, requiring dedicated priority corridors but causing inefficient resource allocation if not coordinated in real time; safety constraints and air traffic management complexity increase. Social equity constraints may impose coverage requirements, as inequitable access reduces both congestion relief and public acceptability. Fixed-route airport shuttle services are considered the first commercially viable use case due to simpler airspace and fewer obstacles. Objective templates: minimize total travel time or operating cost, maximize served demand, minimize fleet size, subject to vehicle capacity, vertiport throughput, airspace corridor availability, repositioning costs, and equitable access thresholds. High operational costs and small vehicle capacity limit mode share; repositioning cost must be traded off against service level gains.

Solution methods include facility-location models extended with 3D airspace constraints, logit-based demand modules feeding optimization, and simulation-optimization loops for operational detail under variable demand.

UAM airspace is a constrained low-altitude three-dimensional envelope with point-to-point short-haul demand and exceptionally high traffic density. Airspace capacity assessment quantifies the maximum safe flight operations per unit time within corridors and vertiport zones, identifying bottleneck areas and conflict hotspots under safety margins. Corridor design is a multi-objective optimization problem (e.g., maximizing throughput while minimizing noise); the FAA proposes three configurations: conventional one-way, corridors with vertical/lateral passing zones, and multi-track corridors with parallel sub-routes. Demand forecasting can be modeled via deep neural networks that capture nonlinear relationships among temporal variables (month, day, time) and environmental factors (temperature, precipitation, wind speed, visibility, air quality), compensating for scarce real data. Operational traffic flow management must coordinate density, departure/arrival timetables, and separation distances. UAM maturity levels (UML-1 to UML-4, passenger transport only at UML-4) can impose phased constraints on cargo versus passenger operations.

Service scheduling (supply-side) sequences eVTOL movements without directly altering passenger choices.

Objectives minimize turnaround time/cost or maximize vertipad utilization. Constraints include no-wait transitions, tight space, and charging requirements that introduce sequence-dependent setup times. JSSP methods are adapted with vertiport-specific no-conflict rules on shared paths. Charging complexity adds real-world complication, suggesting state-dependent processing times in scheduling models.

units.title: Urban Air Mobility: Systematic Review of Scientific Publications and Regulations for Vertiport Design and Operations
units.summary:
The review consolidates vertiport as the term for VTOL ground infrastructure and organizes research into eleven topics, the most modeling-relevant being airspace operations, vertiport design, location and network, and throughput/capacity. Key entities are eVTOL/VTOL aircraft, vertiports with multiple landing pads and ground taxiways, steep/vertical approach-departure corridors, and U-space/UTM services. High-throughput operations demand reduced separation minima, simultaneous autonomous movements, and conflict-free scheduling.

Core problem types: strategic vertiport network design (locating vertiports, sizing pad counts, multi-modal connections); tactical throughput analysis (slot assignment for arrivals/departures under separation constraints); vertiport layout optimization (pad placement, taxi routes). Decision variables include vertiport locations, number of pads, time slots, and trajectory parameters. Objectives typically maximize throughput or minimize infrastructure cost and noise exposure. Constraints involve minimum temporal/spatial separation for safety, pad occupancy limits, ground movement conflicts, weather minima (wind, visibility), and noise contours. Uncertainty sources are weather and demand.

Implementation caution: the majority of studies remain theoretical; integrating realistic operational constraints, safety regulations, and weather resilience is critical. A reusable pattern treats each vertiport as a resource-constrained multi-server queue with separation buffers, coupled to a network location problem.

units.summary: Vertiport design is governed by safety volumes based on a VTOL aircraft’s D-value. The FATO dimensions are multiples of D, and approach/departure surfaces have a 12.5% slope, creating obstacle clearance zones. Procedures for aborted take-off and balked landing require a safe operating volume and a go-around path from the landing decision point back to the landing direction point, effectively forming a closed loop that constrains vertiport footprint and surrounding airspace. Airspace structure is initially limited to 500 ft AGL, with U-space service levels U1–U4 introducing progressive automation and traffic management services. Vertiport traffic management roles, information requirements, and coordination among multiple U-space service providers remain undefined, posing uncertainty for capacity and scheduling models. Optimization models can site and size vertiport elements (TLOF, FATO, parking) subject to surface clearance constraints and go-around path capacity. Decision variables include number and orientation of pads; objectives may minimize land use, delay, or cost while satisfying throughput targets. Uncertainty sources include evolving regulations and missing ConOps for passenger eVTOL operations, which suggests robust or phased capacity planning. Decomposition strategies may be required to handle distributed provider coordination around shared vertiport airspace.

units.title: Urban Air Mobility: Systematic Review of Scientific Publications and Regulations for Vertiport Design and Operations
units.summary: Vertiport infrastructure is characterized by a takeoff/landing area (TLOF), final approach and takeoff area (FATO), and safety area, each sized as a multiple of the VTOL aircraft’s controlling dimension CD. FAA rules set TLOF=1CD, FATO=2CD, safety area=3CD; EASA uses an enclosing circle D with FATO=2D and TLOF based on undercarriage span; international guidelines apply maximum dimension MD with FATO=1.5–2MD. Approach and departure slope constraints (7.1° FAA vs. 12.5° EASA) and vertical segment requirements define obstacle limitation surfaces that restrict vertiport placement. Vertiports act as nodes terminating airspace corridors (below 400–500 ft AGL) managed by UTM service suppliers with dynamic geo-fencing and tactical de-confliction. Core optimization problems include location-allocation to maximize demand capture subject to access/egress time limits, pad number and layout decisions under modular scalability (stackable decks), and charging infrastructure sizing for electric aircraft. Noise contours and community acceptance act as hard siting constraints. Demand must exceed thresholds for profitability; only some city structures provide sufficient density and short ground access. Throughput models must incorporate passenger processing (biometric screening, check-in) and ground movement within the vertiport volume. Because no operational vertiport exists, models must handle regulatory uncertainty, multi-jurisdictional standards, and integration with public transport networks to minimize intermodal transfer times.

units.title: Urban Air Mobility: Systematic Review of Scientific Publications and Regulations for Vertiport Design and Operations
units.summary:
Vertiport is defined as infrastructure permitting electric/hybrid/hydrogen VTOL operations, including charging/fueling/maintenance and passenger buildings; a vertistop disallows those servicing activities, restricting turnaround. Airside key physical entities: at least one Final Approach and Take-Off area (FATO), optionally taxiways and stands. D-value (diameter of smallest horizontal circle enclosing the aircraft in take-off/landing configuration) sizes FATO and obstacle clearance surfaces. Folding-wing configurations introduce D_taxi and D_parking values for ground movement and parking. Obstacle-free volumes (OFV) above pads are prescribed by reference volumes (e.g., Type 1) and may be bi‑/omni‑directional; approach/departure surfaces protect vertical climb segments and transition to forward flight. Stands may be used simultaneously, sequentially, with hover‑turning or taxi‑through, each imposing different space and time constraints.

Operations are stratified by certified category: Category Enhanced requires an alternate vertiport reachable after a critical engine failure; Category Basic may accept a precautionary landing elsewhere. This engenders a reachability constraint linking vertiport network layout to aircraft performance and failure scenarios. Operation types (IFR cargo in controlled airspace, U‑space operations with/without pilot on board) determine allowable airspace classes and performance requirements, affecting vertiport approach path design and obstacle separation criteria. A landing decision point (LDP) defines a required landing distance for safe rejection after engine failure, which must be accommodated in FATO length. Markings (D‑value, maximum mass) enforce aircraft‑infrastructure compatibility checks. Modeling patterns: vertiport sizing and selection subject to D‑value envelopes and OFV dimensions; emergence network design with alternate‑vertiport coverage constraints under engine‑failure uncertainty; stand scheduling with motion‑type‑dependent separation; binary compatibility matrices for vehicle‑pad assignments.

Key constraints: vertiport capacity, maximum vehicle wait time ≤20 min, DNL ≤65 dB noise contours (modeled via Schultz curve over hexagon grids), 95% of flights within 5 min of schedule, and transfer/access time thresholds from ground modes—longer transfers drastically reduce UAM mode share. Demand is derived from commuting heat maps, income-scaled census data, or same-day parcel potential; high-value traveler segments may be prioritized. Service time uncertainties (lognormal/normal for pad occupancy, Poisson arrivals) shift deterministic pad counts upward in simulation-based sizing. Heuristic solution methods—greedy with update steps, elimination heuristics—yield near-optimal networks (91% of optimal) across varied battery ranges, vehicle speeds, and demand scenarios. A reusable pattern aligns vertiport networks to a generic hexagonal highway “wheel-and-spoke” geometry, while integrated simulation frameworks couple demand, vertiport design, airspace routing, and scheduling to assess interdependencies. For parcel delivery, a 10-minute last-mile driving limit bounds vertiport catchment areas.

Mode shift is triggered by time-saving thresholds: ≥25% for long-distance commuters and ≥50% for short-distance commuters. Transfer time (5, 10, 15 min) and catchment radius (e.g., 3 miles) act as parameters; larger radii reduce required vertiport pairs but increase passenger access/egress time.

Airport-adjacent sites are scored on passenger accessibility, obstacle clearance, noise, expandability, and strategic availability. Demand is predicted by mode-choice models using in-vehicle, shuttle, and out-of-vehicle times. Required landing pad (FATO) counts follow peak-hour demand; ground separation ≥200 ft and separate arrival/departure paths with obstacle-free protection surfaces constrain capacity. In controlled airspace, route design via Rapidly Exploring Random Trees minimizes cost subject to incremental distance thresholds from manned aircraft, obstacles, and terrain (e.g., starting at 25 ft). Application at Tampa TRACON found no permanently acceptable airspace volume for VTOL trajectories, showing existing airport layouts and clearance requirements can render vertiport placement infeasible. Integrating such airspace and ground separation constraints into network sizing models is critical.

units.summary:
Vertiport operations distinguish between pads (touchdown/lift-off areas) and gates (boarding/charging). The gate-to-pad ratio is a key design variable, governed by vehicle turnaround time. Turnaround processes include boarding, deboarding, and either battery charging or battery swapping. Short-turnaround designs (2–10 min) assume minimal gate services; long-turnaround designs (30+ min) incorporate full charging and minor MRO. Charging duration and swapping time are critical timing parameters; battery swapping may reduce turnaround but raises fleet-interoperability issues.

UAM flights are structured into pre-flight, departure, en route, approach, landing, and post-flight phases. Strategic planning (pre-departure) must resolve most conflicts via flight schedules, slots, and time buffers. Tactical interventions (in-flight) absorb residual uncertainty through ground/aerial holding, holding patterns, and diversion to alternate vertiports. Short eVTOL endurance (under one hour) and uncertainties such as weather or CNS degradation make precise scheduling essential, with contingency slots and diversion arcs serving as safety constraints.

Optimization models can be two-stage: a strategic phase decides flight-to-slot assignments, gate-pad allocations, and planned buffers, minimizing expected cost or delay; a tactical recourse phase applies holding, resequencing, or diversion given realized disruptions. Capacity limits are defined by pad and gate occupancy, turnaround service times, and airspace separation minima. The gate-to-pad ratio can be modeled as a design variable in a queuing network where turnaround time is the service time. Battery management introduces binary swap/charge decisions per gate, with implications for energy-constrained scheduling. Robust scheduling patterns include time buffers, slot windows, and diversion arcs as recourse actions.

units.title: Urban Air Mobility: Systematic Review of Scientific Publications and Regulations for Vertiport Design and Operations
units.summary:
Vertiport networks serve eVTOL flights with finite FATO pads, parking spaces, and separation minima (horizontal 0.1–1 nm, temporal 45–60 s). Strategic conflicts arise from intersecting trajectories and shared resources among multiple operators; resolution actions include departure delay, speed/direction changes, re-routing, and cruise-speed adjustments. Temporal separation reductions yield larger delay savings (−28 %) than horizontal (−7 %). Scheduling horizon length determines delay composition: short horizons shift delay from ground to airborne, whereas horizons exceeding flight duration keep delay on the ground.

A rolling-horizon traffic-flow management problem decides whether to insert or delay pop-up demands; frequent pop-ups favor insertion. Re-routing airborne vehicles is often omitted. First-come-first-served sequencing captures at least 80 % of throughput but becomes inefficient with many resources. Tactical arrival scheduling assigns required times of arrival and descent angles, absorbing up to three minutes of delay without hovering, with energy-efficient correction in the final cruise leg. Winged and wingless eVTOLs are segregated until a metering fix. Concentric ring structures define terminal airspace; sequence-based and back-queue approaches trade flexibility against conflict frequency, with the former requiring more tactical de-confliction. A decentralized ATM hierarchy groups vertiports into vertihubs, each sector managing its own arrivals/departures and handovers. Contingency planning builds a tree of Dubins-based trajectories to alternate vertiports. FCFS can be replaced by priority based on remaining energy to avoid bottlenecks.

units.summary:
Vertiport placement and orientation must satisfy wind constraints derived from historical data: crosswind ≤10.5 kts in 95% of hours to avoid loss of usability. Operational procedures impose hard limits: no tailwind departures/arrivals, crosswind ≤15 kts. Vehicle capability requirements are set to achieve a target annual operational availability—e.g., headwind withstand of 20 m/s yields 99% operability in Munich; for US metro areas 35 kts gust capability enables 95% availability. A diversion reserve of 10 km is needed to handle weather or charging blackouts.

Weather impact scores (1–10) with a threshold of 3 define reduced operating hours; impacted hours vary by season and location. Micro-urban effects (heat island, channeling, turbulence) demand real-time sensing. Sensor placement optimization must trade coverage against bandwidth/cost, while aircraft-mounted sensors add data but reduce payload.

Turbulence (modeled via Dryden) degrades final approach accuracy, increasing required landing pad size and reshaping approach surfaces. Enhanced vision systems require the FATO to be uniquely distinguishable and fiducial markers within the final 300 m for precise pose estimation.

units.title: Urban air mobility network design and operations strategy in an urban agglomeration
units.summary: Urban air mobility network design is formulated as an MIP that jointly selects vertiports and allocates eVTOL flows. Travel time between vertiports i and j is τ_ij = t_fij + v_gij, where t_fij = t_air,ij + t_w (fixed pre-flight waiting); v_gij = (1−ρ_i)·max(t_gij − t_fij, 0) captures expected detour from ground transport when no eVTOL is available at origin, with ρ_i the availability probability from an M/M/1 vertiport queue. The system is a closed queueing network with total fleet N: vertiport queues (M/M/1), transit queues (M/G/∞), and unproductive repositioning queues (M/G/∞) that balance flows. Demand is sensitive to generalized travel time and cost, scaled by time-sensitivity parameter b. Objective maximizes profit (revenue minus flight, repositioning, and fixed vertiport costs). Constraints include a limit R on vertiports, flow conservation, fleet-size balance across queues, and queueing relations (e.g., ρ_i = λ_i/μ_i). The model approximates the closed network via linear constraints inspired by Adelman (2007). Implementation caution: pre-flight waiting t_w strongly degrades profit, so sensitivity analyses must stress-test t_w. Adding low-demand vertiports improves coverage but can reduce system profitability.

units.title: Urban air mobility network design and operations strategy in an urban agglomeration
units.summary: The design of a UAM network involves eVTOL aircraft, vertiports at multimodal hubs, and passenger mode choice via logit. The problem jointly selects vertiport locations (capped at R), discrete utilization levels ρ ∈ {0,0.05,…,1} (with zero as closure), passenger flows ψ_ij, empty repositioning φ_ij, and integer fleet size Γ. Profit = fare·ψ_ij minus per-trip flight, repositioning, fixed vertiport, and fleet capital costs. Flow conservation requires Σ_j (ψ_ij+φ_ij) = Σ_j (ψ_ji+φ_ji). Passenger demand captured via ψ_ij = (α_ij D_ij)/(n ρ_i), with precomputed maximum flows ̅ψ_ijs for each origin–destination and service level s. The MIP uses binary ω_is for level selection and big-M constraints: ψ_ij ≤ Σ_s ̅ψ_ijs ω_is + W(ω_i0+ω_j0), ψ_ij ≥ Σ_s ̅ψ_ijs ω_is − W(ω_i0+ω_j0), enforcing correct ψ_ij and zero if either endpoint closed. Queueing-based fleet constraint: Γ ≥ Σ_i Σ_s (s/(1−s)) ω_is + Σ_{i,j} t_ij^f (ψ_ij+φ_ij), where the first term is M/M/1 mean queue length. Passenger waiting time from M/M/1 degrades profit strongly. An exact linearization avoids nonlinearity by precomputing tier-dependent flows. Caution: spatial demand aggregation filters trips lacking hubs at both ends; low-demand vertiports may reduce profit; price threshold ~6 ¥/km; eVTOL cost reductions yield nonlinear fleet/profit gains; big-M values must be carefully set; queue parameters must align with service level. Transferable: feedback between layout and queue-sensitive demand; demand filtering with spatial indices; repositioning flows from flow conservation; network cardinality limits affect repositioning; offline tier-capacity precomputation with binary selection and big-M linking.
